utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's Ms. Sartorio. I know the advocacy will match the elevated status we will have been accorded today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I will try not to disappoint you, Your Honour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Hough.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Hough. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry. I made that mistake and it stuck in my head ever since the beginning when I made that mistake. My name is Laurie Sartorio, and I'm a prosecutor here, and I'll be asking you some questions on cross-examination. And since you've testified before, I'm sure you're familiar with being cross-examined. Some of the questions that I'm going to ask you should have either yes or no answers. And I would like you if you would to answer them as concisely as possible because as you heard yesterday, we're limited in our time. So could you try to do that, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll make my best effort.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us yesterday that you have been to Bosnia. When were you there?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there in May of 2000 and -- I believe it was 5 or 6. I'm not quite sure which.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was traveling around the country on a fact-finding trip with a friend, talking with citizens within Bosnia, particularly in Tuzla and Sarajevo. We went to Madressa. We went to an outpatient treatment clinic. We went to a drug and alcohol treatment programme. We went to an NGO. We talked to a lot of people just trying to get a sense of what was the -- in a post-conflict environment, what is the trauma recovery, what resources are available, and generally how are people coping.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Was this a project that you just took an interest in personally, or were you retained by an organisation to do this?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a personal interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say about nine to ten days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to reverse the order of my cross, and I'm going to start with talking about your report and your evaluation of Mr. Lukic. Now, the first thing that I want to talk to you about is related to the issue of translations and the Defence counsel acting as translator. Other than Mr. Ivetic, who acted as your translator, can you tell us who else was present during your interviews?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And at the beginning of your report and, also, you did say yesterday, you shared your concerns that with Mr. Ivetic acting as a translator between you and Mr. Lukic. And am I correct that everything that Milan Lukic said was translated to you and vice versa? In other words, Mr. Lukic does not speak any English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no. A few words but not fluent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And I believe your words that you used yesterday were that it was not the ideal circumstances. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in fact, you didn't talk to the Defence counsel about this arrangement, did you not?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did talk about that arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you probably weren't happy that there wasn't an independent translator?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They assured me this is what we had. All other resources had been exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And that's true. They did assure you that that's all you had, but again, my question was were you not pleased with this arrangement?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't totally dissatisfied. I thought he did a very good job.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But doing a good job, sir, is probably not the same as -- you know, you're subjective. He probably did do a good job, but that's not the point, is it? The point is the objectivity that must be maintained in this type of situation. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, one of the -- ethical conflicts in psychology, fourth edition, are you familiar with that document?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of fourth -- yes, I have that book.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And are you familiar with a section on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who's that by, Ms. Sartorio?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We could bring it up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, why don't you just -- what's the source?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It is the Donald Bursoff. "Ethical Conflicts in Psychology." It's a book on ethical conflicts in psychology, and I was asking if he was familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in this book, in this ethical conflicts book, it said problems may arise when the linguistic skills of the psychologist do not match the language of the client. In such a case, the psychologist referred the client to a mental health professional who is competent to interact in the language of the client. If this is not possible, psychologists offer the client a translator with cultural knowledge and appropriate professional background. If translation is necessary, psychologists do not retain the services -- do not retain the services of translator para-professionals who may have a dual role with the client.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: To avoid jeopardising the validity of the evaluation or the effectiveness of the intervention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed those guidelines that you're referring to, and again, there were really no other choices available. I went through that list from most optimal to least optimal availability, and this is what was available.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm not going to ask you -- I'm not asking you to make a moral judgement about Mr. Ivetic or anything, but my question to you is this: You cannot rule out the fact that items could have been omitted in the discussion between you and Mr. Lukic. You can't rule that out.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you really have no way of confirming one way or the other whether Mr. Ivetic translated everything you said and -- to Mr. Lukic and then back to you other than the tapes; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did you ask for copies of the tapes after your interview?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I can't speak the language.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay, but did you think it was important to maybe have copies of the tapes for your records in case anything were to come up at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't think it was important.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wouldn't serve any purpose for me. I cannot speak the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: True, but you could give them -- you could retain an interpreter back in Kansas, and they could have it translated and transcribed, could they not, if you needed it?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you didn't think it was that important just to have a copy in your office of the interviews?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I knew they had a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And since your interviews, have you listened to the tapes and any parts of the tapes at all?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you ask that the tapes be transcribed and translated?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you learn about the issue with the translator after you arrived in The Hague for the interview or beforehand?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not exactly sure. It would have either been right before I arrived or immediately thereafter. I'm not quite sure on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So it was after you had flown all the way from Kansas to The Hague is when you found out this situation?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may have been right before, but again, it would have been in very close proximity to the flight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, the second area that I want to get into, and it is in regard to the interviews apart from the translation issues, is the cross-cultural issues. And there's some issues that I'd like to talk to you about with regard to the psychological test that you administered. And I understand yesterday you personally recognised these kinds of -- the issues that may arise when you're giving standardised psychological testing across cultures. You recognised that yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more specific with your question what I recognised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. The question was from Mr. Alarid: "Now, what relevance is cultural sensitivity to exploring a forensic path with, let's say, a foreign national of Bosnia?" And you said: "Well, it's very relevant." And then you went on to describe "the differences between groups can often be quite divergent, so it's important to as best one can to try to understand as much as possible about the culture in which you will be immersed," And you went on to describe that. So you were cognizant of problems using psychology tests that I presume these tests were -- they're administered in America; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the scores that are given, that are added up to these tests are measured against Americans; right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them. The Rorschach, for example, is used cross-culturally, internationally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It is?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And has precedent and having been administered to Nazi war criminals who were standing trial at Nuremberg.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So can you tell us what other languages, if you know, that the Rorschach -- is it translated into other languages?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's administered -- the protocol -- or I should say the instrument itself is -- has very low language base to it, so it can be administered in any culture. It's a series of unstructured pictures to which the patient describes what they see. So this has been done, Israel, for example, Mexico, used throughout Europe. There is an international Rorschach society that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But the interpretation of what the patient says as to what he or she sees in the picture, they're measured against American answers; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. I mean, there are American norms, but then other cultures develop their own norms. But the norms that I use and of course the ones that I did apply here were Exner norms that have been developed in the United States, yes, in terms of developing the scores that are then reported, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So the scores on the Rorschach tests that were taken by Mr. Lukic, who is Serbian, his scores were measured against people who take the tests in America?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Oh, may I admit that chapter of that last book, Your Honour, in evidence on ethics?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I had the ERN if you ... 0648 ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P309, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And now I'm going to ask you some questions about another document: Standards For Educational and Psychological Testing, put out by the American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, National Council on Measurement Education, so it's a national -- you're familiar with those standards, are you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You're familiar with some of the issues that are discussed in the standards with regard to cross-cultural psychological testing?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not verbatim, but I know the reference there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What are some of the problems, sir?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of the problems are the same ones that are referenced in the document that you just referred to in terms of the American Psychological Association: Sensitivity to cultural differences, norming issues, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to admit this chapter in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P310, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, with regard to some cross-cultural problems or issues with regard to the particular tests, you admitted yesterday that on the WASI test, which is an IQ test, you said that only the non-verbal tasks were administered since the verbal tasks would have been confounded by language difficulties through translation. That's what -- do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So in reality, the score test is not 100 per cent accurate because you could not administer the entire test.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can get a non-verbal intelligence measure from that, so you don't -- you can get a verbal measurement in a non-verbal measurement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But the test itself, the score is one score, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can get a composite score, which would be the summation of the verbal and the non-verbal, but what I relied on is the non-verbal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that to have a really comprehensive test, you would have to give the whole test.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ideally, but that would assume language compatibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right, and you didn't have that here, so it couldn't be the ideal situation.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I know I mentioned the Rorschach test a minute ago, but particular words that people may use may not mean the same thing from one culture to the next. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in fact, one of the tests that I read recently, in Sweden, I guess they don't have cockroaches in Sweden. Have you heard this story?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So if someone cease a cockroach in another culture on the Rorschach test, well, someone in Sweden would never say that because they don't have cockroaches there. So what I'm trying to get at is the Rorschach is really a verbal test. It depends on the culture, and what the person is seeing from one culture to the next may be different, but that doesn't necessarily mean that that answer from another culture is offbeat; right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the MCMI-III, that's the Million Clinical Multiaxial Inventory. Now, this is a paper-and-pencil test; is it not?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And again, the test is written in English?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And so his answers had to be translated through Mr. Ivetic to you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then, again, the answers to -- his answers were then compared to answers from people in the United States.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And realistically because it is a pencil-and-paper test, it cannot be said with any certainty whether or not the test was working because, again, something could have been lost in translation or something could have been omitted, intentionally or unintentionally. So it can't be said with any certainty that the test was working.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with absolute certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the test, now, you did go to Bosnia and you spoke with a lot of people, and I did read your sojourn to Srebrenica. Do you think, do you have any reason to believe, or do you think that someone from rural Bosnia would respond in the same way that someone might respond in, say, an American psychotherapy session?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Respond to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: To the answers to that test, provide similar responses.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, the WASI test, we just talked about, the IQ test, I'm just curious, why did you give an IQ test to Milan?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I think it's always important to get at least some rough indicator of intelligence, but secondarily to that, the non-verbal components of the test, or in even the verbal, but the non-verbal especially will offer in addition a rough screen for organic problems; for example, on the block design test, patients who tend to demonstrate systematic problems constructing the pictures with the blocks, systematic rotations or reversals with the blocks or stacking the blocks and so on, there are many problems that can arise, begin to alert the examiner that there may be organic problems here, and it's the same with the matrix -- the second non-verbal test was the matrix test. There again, with spatial reasoning and so on, it can raise those questions, so it becomes a rough screen, as well, so it serves two purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you found that -- I believe you found Milan Lukic to have a lower IQ than you expected?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in a way that would not be surprising because it's -- we're only talking about two sub-tests as opposed to a fully administered WASI in American culture, which would have 13 or 14 sub-tests, so it's an extrapolation from that, but I also have to look at -- you have to look at other indicators. Have you to look at his activities of daily living, how he functions, his life history, how he's functioned in the world. Certainly he's not mentally retarded or anywhere close to that. He's not an exceptionally bright man, either, so his generation would fall somewhere in the average to low-average range, and I think that's a fair estimation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: This test also has an aspect to it of effort, so you can measure how hard someone's trying on the test, can't you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not directly other than you can observe effort. If somebody gives up easily, for example, they may not be putting in good effort, if they're reluctant to participate and so on, but by contrast this subject worked up to the best of his ability as far as I could tell. He showed good task perseverance. He worked hard at the task. That tells me that he was putting in effort.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Are there other tests, though, that you can give along with the IQ tests that do test for effort in conducting the IQ test?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the American culture there's one test that I sometimes give. It's called the Validity Indicator Profile which has a way of measuring the degree to which one is putting effort in in comparison to their own capabilities. No, I did not give that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Any reason why you didn't?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I just didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, the Incomplete Sentence Blank Test, again, this is where there's a statement and the person taking the test is asked to complete the sentence; right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And again, I think that you would agree that there has to be some type of, you know, cultural problems with this test, again, because it's based on what the person's upbringing was in life, in everything in their life.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, partly, but, you know, it does have a way of capturing certain attitudes, certain values. It's a useful device.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But in reality -- I mean, you were down in Bosnia. It's very different from the US, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, you also gave the MCMI-III test. This test is not -- this test is somewhat controversial, is it not? It's somewhat criticised.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a lot of the criticism. I mean, one criticism I think that's sometimes levelled is whether or not it's been given to people. It's ideally designed for people who are either in early phases of entering into psychotherapy or have demonstrated some kind of social problem, so the assumption is that it presumes a certain kind of psychopathology on the front end. I'm sure all tests have some body of criticism levelled against them, so this wouldn't be any exception with this test, either, but in my view, certainly the social difficulties he's undergoing are -- would certainly be criterion for social difficulties. I also note that in my own country, the MCMI is routinely administered in correctional settings. When people are first entering into the correctional system and are being screened for major problem which can also determine where they will be assigned in the prison system, so it does have broad utility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And just so you know, your system is my system too.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I just didn't know if you knew I was American.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: There is an article I'd like to ask you about. It's in the Journal of Personality Assessment, 1996, written by a Paul Retzlaff, and it's called: "Diagnostic Validity: Bad Test or Bad Validity Study?" Are you aware of that article?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I -- could you show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sure. It's 0648-8691. It's not a long article. It's just not short. We're not going to read the whole thing. But the author does conclude that the operating characteristics of the test scales are poor in this test.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say, I have not reviewed this article.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We'd like to have it admitted in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P311, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, even -- with regard to this test, even if we accept that the test was accurate given the cultural and possible translation problems, didn't his -- didn't Milan Lukic's responses suggest that he had not been very forthcoming?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are what are referred to as validity scales, and he did show a tendency, if I recall, to be -- as it were, to put his best foot forward, to want to minimise personal short-comings. That, first of all, is not uncommon in an assessment situation. Many people do want to do that. People are applying for a job, for example. But second of all, you do factor that in, and it was -- it did not reach the point where it invalidated the test, but it certainly has to be acknowledged and considered, and I did acknowledge it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But you -- I think your words that you wanted to minimise his short-coming, in your interpretive report, you said his "scores reflect an effort to cover up, a wish fulfillment, not reality. They respond to MCMI-III items as they would like others to see them rather than as they are." So that's a little bit stronger than he wants to minimise his short-comings. It says it's an effort to cover up.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I interpret it as partial cover-up and partial this is a man who wants you to see him in the best possible light.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Oh. Okay. I apologise for that. The interpretive report is actually a computer report that's generated. You didn't write this?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's a computer-generated report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And that's what the computer said, not you. So I'm sorry I attributed that no to you.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But that's what that said, that that was an effort to cover up. So I would say that that's a little bit stronger.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's stronger.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, the Skid test that you gave, that, to your knowledge, has never been validated in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of any tests that are translated into several languages and widely used in Europe and especially in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Balkans, I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't know if you knew what I meant by the Balkans; the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood. Not that I'm not aware of. There may be some, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, there is one, in fact, and it's a very widely used test, the MMPI-II, Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory Test, is translated into Serbian, Croatian.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I remember seeing that being offered in a recent catalog that I received recently, but I didn't know that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If you had, that would have been a much better test to give to Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what about the Psychopathic Check-List Revised? Are you familiar with this test?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's actually the PCLR.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And you're familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And doesn't this test actually measure someone's propensity towards criminal behavior?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, criminal behavior but specifically the focus is on the construct of the psychopathic character.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. So it is kind of geared toward making some type of assessment when there's a hunch that someone may have some psychopathic --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you didn't give this test?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you think about giving this test?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought about it, but I reasoned that since I was going to be giving the SKID, in particular in any MCMI, that with the SKID I would do the screening personality assessment and then I would focus - which I did - specifically on the anti-social personality section, which I did. And had there been data emerging from that section to suggest psychopathy as defined in the PCLR, then I would have been able to zero in on that. But my findings from the anti-social personality section of the SKID did not demonstrate that he met criterion for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the SKID is the interview.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an interview that is administered -- basically, the idea is to ask a series of questions regarding a number of statements, each of which are tagged to various personality disorders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And so the questions that you use in the SKID are very precise?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But when the question's translated, you can't guarantee that it's the same preciseness. Words are different.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, but you have the option to ask the patient to elaborate on their answers, and I did ask him to elaborate on any questions it seemed to me were worth further investigation, and I provided those answers. And review of those elaborated answers, again, assured me that I'm really not seeing the anti-social personality nor the more specific psychopathy construct that I was looking for, and I did keep that in mind that that was something I wanted to be aware of and look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But how long did the SKID take?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I don't recall exactly. I don't know how long it actually took. It's rather lengthy, maybe two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So in two hours, you felt comfortable enough that you had made an assessment that you didn't feel the need to give him a psycho -- a test that's maybe testing for psychopath?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously, I scored it later, but, no -- yeah, you're right. I mean, in that during the time of administration, I was becoming increasingly satisfied that I was not seeing the loading for that personality disorder which I had specifically decided I was going to look for, that in conjunction with the background, the developmental history, and the rest of it was converging for me on the -- the answer that I'm not seeing the anti-social personality or the psychopathy that I had half-way expected to find.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So from that point on, really, the interview was your focus. Everything that you discussed with Mr. Lukic was -- that seemed to satisfy you further as you went along, so you felt -- you didn't have to give any further test, standardized test.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave what I brought. I mean, I could have brought probably a suitcase full of stuff, but I brought what I could carry and what seemed to be reasonable. I had also anticipated that I - wrongly, obviously - that I would have the opportunity to revisit this evaluation with Mr. Lukic, the purpose of which would be to, if needed, give more testing, and that's always a possibility, or to -- and I specifically entertained that I would be able to focus more specifically on gaps, and there were gaps, on contradictions, and there were contradictions, there always are, to try to resolve them and loose threads that may have been there. But up at least until the time of the war, I feel like I was able to get from him a very detailed history with a view towards looking at major indicators of psychiatric disturbance or emerging psychopathy or anti-social personality trends and so on, and I was satisfied that I was not seeing that. And it's generally the case that with these kinds of diagnoses that I was looking for, that you would begin to see indicators of it sometimes really quite young. And even one of the criterion that needs to be met for the anti-social personality disorder specifically is that there have to be indicators before the age of 15, and often there are, juvenile delinquency and conduct problems and so on. That wasn't evident there. So it didn't seem inconsistent that I was not finding it from the assessment, either, because the background was confirming that it's not evident by background -- by self-reported background history, and it's not being reflected in the testing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And I think the operative word there, and we'll talk a little bit more in detail about the interview, but it's the self-reporting interview.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. And -- now, I want to pick up on a couple of things. That was a very long answer, and I do agree that you had a lot of materials. I'm still going through your five binders of research material, and I'm very impressed. But you did say you were hoping to have the opportunity to come back. What was that all about? Was that part of the original discussion?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only in vague terms because the understanding with the attorneys is, you know, Go home, look at your data, write your report, and see where you're at. And that's pretty standard operating, but my practice and it seems to be pretty much routine in capital cases, and I would consider this a capital equivalent, certainly, to have multiple opportunities to revisit with the client for a number of reasons, one of which, obviously, is to resolve contradictions, lingering un-opened questions. The other is that you need multiple points of assessment. You need a -- basically a kind of repeated measures, opportunity to see them in various points in time. Now, I did have that to some degree here. I saw him on six different occasions, but I would really classify that as one large observational point in time. But in my typical work in capital cases, I do have the opportunity to go back after some break in time because I want to have time to review the data. I want to think about it. I want to look at other literature that's relevant. I want to metabolise it, so to speak, and then to go back with a more focussed approach. The first time around is just to get a base-line assessment of where has he been in life, what are his relationships, all that. But the second time around, with a view towards eventually I want to get -- ultimately, I want to get to the crime scenes, because that's what everybody really wants to know, and that's what I want to know. But you cannot get there right away because the risk of pushing too fast on that is you lose the rapport with the client, and sometimes if you push too hard or you become too driven to get there, you lose the client. They will shut off, and you'll never get it. So there is a technique. Have you to be -- you have to work slowly, develop rapport with a view towards this is where you do want to get, and that was my hope.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge David has a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: In your report as well in your answers today, you have discussed the concept of life histories.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: And I imagine that you are aware of various types of life histories.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: And I imagine that you are aware of various types of life histories. One, from a phenomenological point of view, also, you said yesterday phenomenology. And are you in a clinic that Wisbanger has been very important, in [indiscernible] in other phenomenologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: In a pure narrated sequence as you have done, you could capture only a very limited set of meanings, especially when we are doing this interview in a trans-cultural setting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: There are other life histories, and you could remember the work of Sutherland, "The Confessional Thief" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that Jacques Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: -- the achievement of Sanchez in the anthropological literature in which the subject, the director of the experiment is not receiving by the social participant observer. As a matter of fact, Louis [phoen] accompanied that family for various times of the year in the children of Sanchez, and Sutherland interacted with Chuck Conway, the subject of his book in Chicago many times. So there are differences between a certain narrated story and the story that this Chuck is strategically at points was outside the [indiscernible] the insights obtained in the interview. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. However, I'm limited as to how far I can fully immerse myself into the world of the subject here. I mean, in a full phenomenological investigation, you know, I might have lived in his home and spent time with -- living with his family and so on. This was a very circumscribed set of -- situation in which to evaluate a man. He's a captive in prison --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: We understand the limitation, but I just wanted to propose to you that there are other types of life histories in the scientific literature of anthropology and sociology, comparative psychology, and so on. The second component is this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm looking for the reference. I don't seem to be able to find it at the moment, but I'm aware that the American psychiatrist who was assigned to the detention block to provide medical and psychiatric services to -- this was during the Nuremberg trials -- to the defendants wrote a series -- or actually wrote a book about that, but he had literally months to spend with these men, interacting with them on a daily basis, and I think I guess ideally to really get to the bottom -- to try to get that sense of understanding of the kind of questions perhaps all of us struggle with, that's what you would need, and this was certainly a first effort, but the limitations are very clear, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: A third question, and I will not, you know, continue, but it's just for purpose of my own clarification. You have discussed the problem of lack of boundaries nonetheless in times of war. In your report you say that when institutions disappear, the force of law -- when the force of law breaks down, and then conflicts, especially ethnicity conflict takes over. You are talking about in a specific situation of great ennui in the word of [indiscernible]. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if I understand the word you use as ennui.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Ennui --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. I think it even went beyond that kind of ennui indifference. It became a ruthless climate of relentless struggle for survival. And the -- one of the new ways of thinking about conflict in the world that I've become aware of is that many of the conflicts now and in the future will likely be along ethnocentric lines. That is, rather than state versus state, it will be cultural group versus cultural group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: But there is a precaution, as you know Binswanger himself said in his book, "Selective Papers," Harper & Row, page 204 in New York, to say that we are carried away by the forces of destiny including this great conflict situation is only one side of the truth. The other side is that we determine or serve those courses as our destiny, which is saying that even in situation of extreme acute conflict, men still have some capacity to select, to choose, which is to say that over the unconscious forces that drives you to the conflict, there are some who still could exercise reason. Are you agreeing with this quotation? You think that everything is -- there are forces that could not be stopped or redirected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would probably be overly reductionistic to assume that behavior in the climates that we're talking about are either due to -- entirely due to personality problems or entirely due to the environmental disintegration problems. In reality, it's somewhere -- there's a mix there, and I agree there is an existential component here of man is still responsible for his actions, and he cannot always control the factors -- the situations that he finds himself in, but he is responsible for making decisions, but -- and I will be talking about this later, but we also know from research that there are certain social conditions that can be so compelling that it's the exceptional man who can resist not going along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: In your report, you said in relation to Milan Lukic does not of a formal psychotic level under a structure conditions, he will have more difficulty thinking clearly and perceiving understanding people and events realistically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: And in another parts of your report, you call him very much a person who will be oriented from the group, not from himself, that he will have a great propensity to the lines of authority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: If you have to categorise him following Richmond's traditional personality types from the traditionally directed, inner directed, and outer directed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's outer directed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: He's outer directed, which is to say that the more important that his own ego will be the pressure from the group. This is a characterization of reasoning. Are you saying so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just explain again, outer-directed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding of that term, sir, would be if you ask the question about locus of control, that is, is a person more inclined to listen to and follow the dictates of what is going on themselves, inside their head, versus the dictates and the pull from outside? Is a person more inclined to go along with what is socially -- what is socially expedient, what is socially relevant, what is going around, what is the social norm versus an internal set of norms? And this man, I have argued, is a man who's far more inclined to go with what has been externally provided in terms of norms of behavior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand. Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, my questions are a lot more mundane and not quite as interesting and probing, but speaking of -- now I'd like to move on to what you just alluded to, which is what you seem to have found from your interviews with Mr. Lukic. Now, your interview lasted 24 -- approximately 24 hours over a 6-day period?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but to be quite fair to the time-frame, that would count -- it wouldn't be quite that much when you start factoring in just getting access to the facility and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: So let's call it 19 to 20 hours, you know, in terms of actual in-room time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And I noticed at the beginning of your report that you did tell us that you shared -- you told Milan Lukic that your report might be shared with others at the Tribunal, officers of the Tribunal, and you also say in your report that you explained to him and he acknowledged that the usual patient-examiner privilege does not exist in that situation.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So he knew at the beginning of the interview that anything he said could be given to the Prosecution, the judges, the Court, right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would think that that would have been very obvious, yeah, but I did tell him there's no confidentiality here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say it would have been very obvious, I think -- you told him that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him I'll be writing a report, it'll go to the attorneys who will share it with the officers of the Court. I may be called upon to provide testimony about anything from this evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you also took extensive notes --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: -- during your interview. And I notice in your report, and we've counted them up. You have 194 direct quotations of Milan Lukic in your report.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So you did cite -- a lot of your report is just verbatim what he told you.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to get citations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you get those down in your notes or did you go back over the tapes? I believe you said --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No tapes. It's just my furious scribbling at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were compiling your report -- anyway, with regard to the interview, I also want to say that, again, one point I didn't -- well, strike that. Prior to your interview, did you ask for materials to review, or did the lawyers just give you materials?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked them to send me anything they possibly had about this man that in particular -- well, in particular, that it would have any kind of relevance to his background, to his psychiatric history, educational records, just anything that I would always want to see in forensic evaluation. I wanted to know as much about his life as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But normally when you examine or evaluate someone, do you ask them to provide you with the materials, or do you research it independently?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I usually get those materials from the attorney.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: From the attorney, okay.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, occasionally someone might come in and want to hand me something extra, but by and large the bulk of the materials is from the attorney.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what would you consider important documents that you would want to see in this case in evaluating Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd want to see -- well, I guess just right from the beginning, if all this were available, I'd want to see school records, health records, any records from psychiatric contacts, juvenile justice. I'd want to see military records. I'd want to see work reports from employers. I think I mentioned school, academic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Criminal records.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, criminal records. I'd want to see anything at all that can document the kind of man and how he has functioned in various roles in his life at any point in his life, but it's very difficult to often get a comprehensive set of records that provide a true longitudinal picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you receive all the -- those types of materials that you just mentioned prior to your interview?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I received the complaint, an amended complaint, a document describing command structure for the military. There was a handful of small, miscellaneous items, but nothing really comprehensive. There really wasn't much that I could say. This has given me at least the beginnings of some picture of who the man is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when you received those documents, did you contact Defence counsel back and say, I need more information?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I mean, I don't know how often, but I would occasionally say, Give me what you've got.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And did you get any further documents before the interview?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may -- I'm not sure, but I don't -- if I did, it wasn't much, so I really went in -- I guess the term would be rather unvarnished. There just wasn't a lot to go on at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So -- then there probably was not a lot to confront him with, either.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, other than I had obviously read the indictment, so I knew the magnitude of the allegations, which in itself is a major confrontational point. But I didn't have the other records that would have begun to flesh out more completely the life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you didn't have any witness statements or any other facts -- when you say the allegations -- the allegations in themselves are major confrontations, but that's true, but that's just a -- you know, an indictment is just a bare-bones --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, to clarify, what I meant by that is that's the elephant in the room. No matter what he tells me about his life, we still have to get to the allegations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. Okay. And did you get to the allegations?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made several attempts to -- in a broad way because I knew that we're not going to get this fleshed out this time around, just for example, to say, How do you understand this, that I have a pile of -- I have a stack of allegations, and what does this mean? I mean, how can I reconcile this? And the standard, I guess to nutshell, would be that's not true. But that was not a surprising answer, either, first time around.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And subsequent to the interview, did you do any -- did you ask for anymore materials, or did you look for anymore materials to corroborate what he told you or didn't tell you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying after the interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still didn't have much. I mean, what I was ultimately forced to do was to try to look at in terms of written materials. I mean, you rely on open sources, which are highly unreliable, journalistic accounts and so on, and there are many; read as much as I could about the broader political and historical context. I read books in that area, but all that -- but what that -- it's helpful. It's useful to do that because you have to dig in and try to get a sense of the broader historical context, but it doesn't -- all that can tell you is really the world into which this particular man had been immersed, but it doesn't tell me specifically about that particular man, but that's where I had to start.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. Okay. That's fair enough, but you didn't have any -- you didn't get anything else from -- well, you did at some point get some other documents, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had -- when I came for the evaluation last November, it was at that time that I then had the opportunity to begin to review documents relevant to the three witnesses whose records I provided an analysis of, but that was while I was here. So I would evaluate Mr. Lukic in the morning, and then in the afternoon spent the rest of the day looking at the documents. So it was concurrent as this was going on, so I was aware that here are the witnesses, here are the documents relating to those witnesses, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So you -- but all you got were the records of the three witnesses that you were asked to review. You weren't given witness statements, other witness statements or other witness testimony from the trial?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I looked at a statement by the brother of VG-114, and I believe that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But it was strictly what they chose to give to you, the Defence attorneys?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, they have volumes of records.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. And --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to be selective. At some point, have you to decide what you're going to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: True, but it seems to me that if they had volumes of records, if there were other documents that could have shed some light to help you in your analysis, that it would have been important for you to have.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had been available, I would certainly have looked at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you make a request for any types of documents other than what you said, the school records and criminal records and things like that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I requested -- I mean, and these would be standard documents that I would want to look at in any evaluation. Psychiatric history, certainly, but all the other things that I've enumerated, and they just aren't available.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's what they said, they're not available?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever ask Milan Lukic if he ever killed anyone, and meaning out of the war context?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the war context or within --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, within the war context, but not engage in the armed conflict; kill a civilian.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, and he told me he did not kill civilians. He did acknowledge that in a combat context, he did take lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- so really, in reality, the bulk of your report, other than the psychological test, it boils down to what Milan Lukic reported to you.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And I think this is obvious, but given -- in light of your evaluation, you're not able to say -- you're not able to aid the Court in whether he has a certain personality type or doesn't have that personality type, predisposed to committing crimes. You really can't say that based on your evaluation?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say I guess in a qualified way that based upon the available information I have at this point that I am reasonably confident that I'm not seeing the indicators that would support a diagnosis of -- and there are several kinds of diagnoses that you would be expecting to find for someone who would perpetrate a crime, a series of crimes like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But again, the bulk of your data has come directly from the subject himself?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in terms of your report, did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that unusual in your work, that all of the data would come from the subject himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there will always be contradictions, sir, but what is unusual, more typically when I'm dealing with someone who's been accused of serious criminal acts, and I'm talking specifically about violent acts, homicide, and so on, there will be prominent indicators that will be readily apparent from the developmental history when you take their life history, they'll be right there in various combinations, but you will see certain indicators that already tell you that they are on a path towards destruction later on in life, beginning from maladjustment in childhood, through school relationships as a child, and then up through their adolescence, and so on. You can already begin to see the markers that show in retrospect they were already moving in this direction. I'm not seeing those markers in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that's what Ms. Sartorio meant. Ms. Sartorio, were you trying to find out whether he was able to gather information about Milan Lukic from other people?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I wanted to know if you got any information from any other independent source other than Milan Lukic himself.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, I understand your question. And normally that is my practice to do that as much as possible, to get collateral third-party input, objective as possible. I considered family, for example, and the Defence team does have some contact with some family members, I'm told. I've never met them. I looked at that possibility and realised that what I would probably get from family members would be a relatively self-serving report. They would tell me all that's good and perhaps obscure the negative. So I can't really rely on that. I considered friends, people who might know him well, if they were available. My understanding is that the people -- the two friends that he had who knew him relatively well, both have been indicted, Mr. Vasiljevic, and his cousin, Sredoje Lukic. I considered, well, what about policemen or soldiers who knew him at the time of the conflict? My understanding is that all of them are either unavailable or potentially under indictment, so that wouldn't be possible. You keep going down the list. At some point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're out. You're out of options.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. If you would consider as relatively self-serving reports from family members and friends, Ms. Sartorio might want to ask you how much more would you consider reports from the accused himself self-serving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you want me to answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, obviously that's a risk, sir, that an accused might be self-serving, but by and large I had no other collateral sources to really turn to. Family might have been able to support early development and so on, but my understanding is that the family was not in the Visegrad or at least not involved with Mr. Lukic at the time, so I don't think that they would have had a perspective on -- of the accusations other than what they've been told. I even considered UN detention personnel, but the best they would have been able to offer is current adjustment, maybe current health issues, how he's adjusting to gaol, but that doesn't give me the longitudinal perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, Dr. Hough, really, in reality you had, I think, three problems; one is the bulk of the analysis, it was self-reporting on the part of Milan Lukic, that's one; and, two, his lawyer who is bound, ethically bound to have his interests, best interests and his actions; and then, three, you've got the translation problem. My question to you with regard to the second aspect, if Milan Lukic had told -- had answered a question or said that he had killed millions of Bosnian civilian Muslims, in June and July of 1992, do you think his lawyer from an ethical standpoint would have been able to tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question; objection to the hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness is an expert, and we're able to put hypothetical questions to the expert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understand your question right, would the attorney been able to divulge that, had there been a disclosure of that nature, a very self-indicting disclosure, that probably would have put him in a conflict, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in terms of your report - I keep saying that, but I want to get -- did you do a draft report first and then submit it to Defence counsel and then get feedback and then submit another report?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: How was it that you were contacted by the Defence? Did they contact you or ...

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually, I contacted Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Oh. Okay. And for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was interested in becoming involved in work at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you know Mr. Alarid personally?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not out -- no. Well, I mean outside the work in this case, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So how did you -- you just decided to pick up the phone and -- you picked a Defence attorney or you watched on the internet or ...

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean -- no, no. I have a good friend in Topeka, Kansas, named Mr. Kirk Kearns [phoen], and he knew that I was interested in this kind of work, and he gave me a name of a firm in Chicago, and I talked with them, Mr. Ostojic, and Mr. Ostojic said, Why don't you calm Mr. Alarid? He's got a case. And so I did. I went to see him, and we agreed to work together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, did you -- when you made that first contact, did you -- so you offered your services in what capacity? Did you tell him you would examine his client for competency? Or what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told him, you know, I'm a psychologist, and this is the kind of work I do, and if you need -- if there are issues that are relevant, that I can provide services.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And that's probably not the usual way that you get involved in forensic cases, is it?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but sometimes you have to knock on a door.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair. Now, I'm going to talk about the substance of the report. Part of the purpose of your report, and I think it's up-front, was to obtain his "views regarding actions during the Balkan war in Visegrad." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And on page 11 of your report, you state: He did not feel the tension of emerging war. Such tensions may have been experienced by the people who lived there, but not for him." Do you remember writing that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Can you direct me specifically, though, so I can track with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can we put the report on the screen? It might facilitate the Court following along as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We have it uploaded as 1D22-0735.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The end of the third paragraph -- first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: End of the first paragraph. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Page 11.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is that page 11?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you scroll down, please. Sorry I had it typed up in my notes. It's the last sentence of the first paragraph. "He did not feel the tension of emerging war. Such tensions may have been experienced by the people who lived there but not for him."

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to go to page 24. The third paragraph. You're talking about the friends -- "once the war began, all his friends began to gravitate to their respective ethnic sides. Many people heard the propaganda and subsequently went to war for their own representative groups." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this kind of seems contradictory to me, so which is it? Did he feel the tensions, or did he not feel the tensions?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that when he went to visit his family in Visegrad in January that he wasn't feeling the tensions yet. He went to the store run by a Muslim family; the lady was very nice to him; she saw his license plates; he was from Belgrade, the car; she let him use his phone; tensions were emerging, but he wasn't feeling it. This description in Zurich when the young men were beginning to watch the television scenes and so on, he described how they began to diverge into their various groups. I mean, the tensions were obviously there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But he minimised them in terms of himself?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, you know, I would say I was quite surprised how slow he seemed to have been to really grasp the gravity of war is coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you just believed him because that's what he told you.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his descriptions were consistent across time, and he sort of laughed at himself, you know: How could I have been so naive?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Another question to you is when he talked to you about the White Eagles, I noticed that yesterday you were testifying about that, and it seems like he described them in quite some detail, that the White Eagles consisted of approximately 50 to 80 individuals, and he knew their commander, and on and on. Did you ask hm him how he knew so much about the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you know that that was an allegation in the case, that he's a member or works in groups that have committed crimes with the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were you aware of it at the time you interviewed him?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So did you probe late bit more?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would object to the question as misstating the evidence. He was alleged to be the leader of the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me. Yes. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But did you probe that further because it is a part of the case. Did you know that before the case?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew it before the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And so when you start talking about this, did you sort of hone in on this?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that point. I'm not sure why other than I may have been saving it for a return back to the topic, but I wanted to get kind of a base-line description from what he was telling me about the way things were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also say in your report, and again, after the age of 15 the only legal problems he has had are the current one related to the ICTY. Do you remember saying that, or do you want to find that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, I remember. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you still -- has that changed?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of legal problems before the age of 15?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: After the age. It says after the age.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. That must be a mistype. I apologise to the Court. It should read before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I'm veering specifically on the anti-social personality diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So you need to make that correction then on the record that that it's supposed to be before the age of 15.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me what page that's on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Page 8.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The second paragraph. The second sentence in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me correct, then. No, that would be correct. After the age of 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Sartorio, while you're looking things up. I'm a bit at a loss, and I'm sorry because I wasn't able to be present yesterday, but I'm wondering where this is leading us to, this part of the evidence, which I think is very interesting from an academic point of view, but what does it help? Does it now have any relevance for us to assess the criminal responsibility of the accused? Does it say something about the mens rea or -- I'm just trying to understand why we need this evidence and whether we should pursue with it. Could the parties help me with this? Mr. Alarid, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'd prefer not to comment on where the Prosecution is going on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It's your witness. You brought the evidence, so I would wish to know from you why you were bringing this evidence and what the relevance of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The relevance is within the confines. I understand the Prosecution's objections, and it's always an issue of weight. But within the confines of what this expert was able to achieve in the psychoanalytical setting, with all those strengths and weaknesses conceded, it simply is to assess this human being, and I think he's done so, whether it's from a leadership versus ordinary man perspective, whether it's from an intelligence to an above-intelligence perspective. And also in hopes of giving you a little bit more of a cultural perspective of this individual, where he came from, what were the social factors that were involved in who he was. I mean, we've seen some pictures of him as a young man, but very little to be able to tie that together to help you assess because I think it is important to asses this individual's capacity for leadership, his intelligence because the allegations at the front side were so specific. He wasn't alleged to be a member of the White Eagles. He was alleged to be the leader of the White Eagles, so much so that his 8-year-senior cousin, a formal police officer, would fall into rank step behind him, and that's how this case was originally pled. Now the theories of liability may have changed over time, but as alleged, that was important, and I think that that's what we were attempting to accomplish and differentiate from the theory presented by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alarid, but with all respect I think we're spending a lot of time on this, and we've got your message, and I would really wish to proceed in a faster space.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well -- okay, Your Honour. The first part with regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, but I have to react related to those allegations, which I just heard from my friend Mr. Alarid related to the 8-years-older cousin. Thank you very much, just for the record. Nothing further. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I maybe have 10, 15 minutes more on the report. I mean, I feel that if the Court's going to accept the report in evidence, then we have to do our job and put in what we feel the report -- the issues with the report, so I realise it's not -- it goes to sentencing, perhaps, mitigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: That's the only thing I can see in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: But to assess the mens rea, I don't think this is going to help us very much. So if you could please restrict yourself to the minimum. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I will. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
