utterances.text: Before you proceed, may I -- because you had asked me about the age 15, I just want to clarify. After having looked at the document, it would be correct as it stands, so I would apologise for the misstatement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So it is after the age of 15.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No problem. Now, in the group of materials, you noticed that there was a judgement against Milan Lukic and three other perpetrators, and the judgement says that they tortured violated life and person, murdered civilian persons, and it's about stopping a bus carrying Bosnian Muslim men, ordering them at gun-point to get off the bus, and then proceeding to abuse them physically, beating them with wooden sticks and then finally killing them. He was convicted of that crime, and in the materials you gave to us the other evening, I noticed you have the judgement.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. You know, I remember us talking about the bus incident. I don't remember having reviewed that document, but if it's in my file, I obviously did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'd like to admit the Severin judgement into evidence, Your Honour. It directly contradicts a report of the expert, and it was received in response to an RFA, and I have the RFA here int he response. It's perfectly -- it's an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the Severin judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The Severin judgement was a judgement that was obtained in absentia while Mr. Lukic was out of the country and also under indictment for this particular charge. It was never defended; he was never arrested on it. And so from the standpoint of his participating in the legal process, I understand the point the Prosecution's making, but attempt to admit the judgement through this witness is improper, and it's an improper attempt at introducing character evidence in showing of the consistency and pattern of conduct that is not supported by the evidence. We would have to have an additional trial within a trial to explore the Severin issue, and that would be a waste of the Court's time considering that we are focussing on the specific dates in June of 1992 as opposed to anything that was obtained in absentia without the benefit legal counsel defending him and with this person being present, and he does have a right to request to retry that case in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the judgement speaks for itself. You can give it whatever weight you want, but it does contradict the report, and Mr. Hough had this in his possession, and it didn't factor into his report, and I think that it speaks for itself in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then she can cross him with that and for the implications that that has to his report, but why do we need this extraneous material that has no relevance on the charges today?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hough had the judgement?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P312, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And now, there's just a couple more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: 0644-6149, please. Could the court usher please bring that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And while that's coming up on the screen, on page 31 of your report, and that's the whole subject of your report, you drew the conclusion that Milan Lukic is quote "clearly a follower, not a leader." That's your conclusion; right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And as soon as this document ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And could we go to the second page of the report. Well, actually, go to the first page. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you see that this is a record of interview with the accused and then -- you'll see down on the right, it says Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you direct me with the scroller?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you just highlight the top portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: On 30 October 1992, and it goes on, it's a record of interview with Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, could we go to the second page, please. Sorry, page 3. I apologise. Page 3. Sorry, Your Honours. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, it's a long paragraph, but I'd like you to read, and I could read it out loud, but I would like to admit this document in evidence. Would you read the paragraph, sir? "I finally returned from Germany ..."

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. "I finally returned from Germany, or rather, from Switzerland, on 10 April this year when the conflict began between the Serbs and the Muslims in Bosnia. I reported to the Visegrad Territorial Defence Staff in order to participate in Serbian combat operations for the liberation of Visegrad. I have been engaged continually in combat activities ever since. "I was a member of the Obrenovac Detachment, which is a special unit attached to the Visegrad SUP. Since the group was composed of people from the outskirts of Visegrad who mostly lived in Serbia, we had special training. We were later attached to the Visegrad Territorial Defence as a company of volunteer guards called Osvetnik/avenger. I was and still am the commander of this detachment. Usually, the detachment had 25 to 50 members, but the composition fluctuated, as some members left and new ones joined." That's the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, does the fact that he says in that recorded interview here he was the commander, doesn't that suggest to you a leadership position and not a follower?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I wondered about that. Was that document signed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, you have the English version and --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. That's what he told the people who were interrogating him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you didn't include that in your report?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I hadn't read that document until after.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But after you read it, you didn't amend the report?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to have this document admitted in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I believe it was admitted --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Not this one. I don't believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: This was admitted in the OTP case when the officer --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, that's another one. We're getting to that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it. If we discover we've already admitted it, then we'll deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My case manager with check.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's admitted as Exhibit P313, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could the court officer please bring up 0422-4603.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Sartorio, in the document we have just admitted --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- what it said is that he was and still is the commander of a detachment. That's of a military unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. This document right here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the one we just admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said. It was his -- it was an interview of Milan Lukic where he said he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you would want to say that that contradicts --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- the leadership claim?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, as well as -- yes. And the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't believe that that is how I understand the argument in the indictment that he's a leader, a leader of a paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, certainly, he wasn't -- our position is that he was not a follower; he was not a passive follower, which I think is the conclusion reached, so we do dispute that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe that they are different qualities entirely, being a commander of a military detachment and an allegation that one has leadership attributes based specifically on a claim that one is a leader of a paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe the army factor, I believe the army factor makes that claim invalid, but the fact that you are a commander of a contingent to my mind doesn't necessarily mean that you have leadership attributes. You may, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right, but I think also the point is that Dr. Hough did admit to reading this document, and he did not -- it's not a criticism of the doctor. He wanted to see the accused again, but he did not confront the accused with that and ask him about it. And I think that that goes to the credibility of the report issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The document in front of us, as you can see, it's a military certificate, and it's a certification that Milan Lukic is the commander of a sabotage and Reconnaissance group. Now, I would submit that a commander of this kind of special unit group particularly would have qualities of a leader and not a follower. This seems like a type of special forces group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, assumes facts not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We'd like this admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it. Let move on quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P314, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, Dr. Hough, you would agree with me, though, that, these documents may appear to contradict what Milan Lukic told you.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the second document, the certificate, I haven't seen that document before. I haven't studied it or tried to put it into context, so the answer I would give you would be qualified, but on the face of it, it would seem to contradict that, but it also supports in my understanding his claim that he had always been within the command structure of the military and not outside of it. The paramilitary would be -- my understanding would be outside the command structure, the more of a rogue element.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you're not sure because you -- did you study --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I study this document? It's the first time I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right, but you didn't study the military structure of the Bosnian and Serbian Army?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at it, but it was pretty complicated, so I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I agree. I totally with you. Okay. Just one last point. There's a part of your report -- well, you mention that he said he was the president of the veteran's association and that all five local commanders voted him in, and that there were thousands of soldiers scheduled to vote.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they tell me, or a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Again, to me, this appears to be an inconsistency. You're the president of a thousand-man organisation. Is that the quality of leader or a follower?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what he told me is actually he'd been nominated to be president but he declined and conferred that leadership position to someone who was an attorney, that he'd been nominated because of his actions as a soldier. That he'd been recognised as a pretty heroic combatant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But I don't believe you said that in your report that he was nominated and stepped down. I believe you said he was elected. I have a direct quote.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. What page?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Page 23.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So it's the second paragraph under section 5, After the War.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: This is my last question, Your Honours, on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So you said he was --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reading is that he'd been offered the position. He'd turned it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I'm sorry. I do apologise. That's next.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Is it time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll take this opportunity to deal with some administrative matters. First, Mr. Alarid, your request for Marie O'Leary to examine Cliff Jenkins, can you tell us about her qualifications?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. She's a licensed attorney, licensed since 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In Minnesota, to practice before the bar in Minnesota. She's practiced with the public defender's office, but she came out here and engrained herself in the system, of which she's spent the lion's share of her career, in the support roles of legal assistant. She was also the head of the ADC, the administrative head of the ADC, and then transferred to -- she's currently assigned to the Djordjevic case, and that's why she had to leave our case because of the time constraints and the start-up of Djordjevic, in which she had previously engaged, but we had thought that this would be over before trial actually started, and that's why you haven't seen her for the last month and a half or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that a similar procedure was followed in the Milutinovic case. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. I had one of my legal assistants Mr. Boris Zorko lead one of our Defence witnesses, and I believe Mr. Ackerman had Ms. Nadia Zed cross-examine one of the OTP witnesses in that proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to allow it in the exceptional circumstances. We want to ensure that you have as much time as possible, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: To be honest, this would give me some time to do some housekeeping because a lot of things have come down, and there's a lot of short-term deadlines that we're trying to keep -- including trying to get our subpoena witnesses here for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For example, the Trial Chamber would hope that it would give you enough time to proof Milan Lukic for Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: To begin putting him on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, we don't -- to be honest, Your Honour -- and I wish it were different. In my town, you can go visit in the gaol on the weaken. Here, you cannot, and it's against the UNDU policy, so with tomorrow's double session and Mr. Ivetic being my sole source to the language, we're probably pretty much obligated to be here, even with Marie conducting the exam, so I wouldn't be able to give you that kind of quality proofing by Monday, Your Honour. I think that would be unrealistic, definitely unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In that case, who would you have on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Right now, Your Honour, two -- we have confirmed two of the subpoena witnesses, and we're trying to facilitate getting them here, but interesting, the VWS says we have to submit the WIF information for witnesses that really are subpoenas, so they're not under our umbrella of influence in any way, shape, or form. So we're trying to figure out how to get them here in short order. But other than that, Your Honour, with Mr. Jenkins concluding and absent Mr. Lukic, we would not have witness for Monday, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Seems a terrible waste.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And potentially we could close our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or you could close your case on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I mean, that's a possibility without -- well, no, that's not true. We need the subpoenas to come. We do need those two witnesses that we've got confirmation on, but I'm concerned because there's really not a system in place for Defence to bring subpoena witnesses. It's just a void, if you will, in consideration, and so we're trying to bridge that gap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: With regard to Marie O'Leary, I should tell you that my -- you will be contacted in relation to the power of attorney that's to be provided. Somebody will be contact to give you assistance in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now I must also say that the Chamber is making arrangements to sit full days, morning and afternoon from now until the end of the trial, subject, of course, to minor possible changes. And of course, you know that there is no hearing on Tuesday, the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Hillary's in town, I take it. That's what I've heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Milan Lukic's case will therefore end on Friday, the 3rd of April, if he testifies. If he does not, then this may be moved up to Wednesday or Thursday. That time-frame, of course, will allow for consideration of the pending motion to amend the Defence witness list plus the two confirmed subpoena witnesses. And then, rebuttal and rejoinder, Monday the 6th to Wednesday the 8th of April. Chamber witnesses and housekeeping matters, Thursday the 9th of April. Filing of final briefs by all parties, Wednesday the 15th of April. The closing arguments are set for the 21st of April. And pursuant to the order of the 11th of March, each party has been allotted one hour unless otherwise determined by the Chamber. Now, Mr. Groome, yesterday I had said to you, get Dr. Will Fagel. But on further reflection, it seems to us that the better course is only to hear him in your rebuttal case proper because he is to testify about five documents allegedly signed by Risto Perisic, and that's a subpoena witness. We are not certain whether he's coming. Then a map of the Drina River allegedly written by Milan Lukic. Of the five documents, one is in evidence, and the map will only be admitted if a particular witness testifies, so it would seem to be waste of the Court's time to hear Fagel before the documents are admitted. So I trust that will not be a severe inconvenience for you, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will contact him, Your Honour, he's given me some available dates, but I need to check back now that I have these new dates, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber will have to request expedited responses to pending motions, and I set them out as follows. Let us deal with this in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio, my colleague is urging speed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will endeavor to speed along. I have fewer questions on this part than the first part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, Dr. Hough, now I'd like to turn your attention to the three letters that you wrote to Mr. Alarid about three of the Prosecution witnesses. That's the -- it will be -- the remaining questions of you will be based on these letters. And again, yesterday you said you had never met or spoken with any of the witnesses; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. And therefore, it follows that you have never had evaluation of them in order to do a proper diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So you're not really able to say to the judges to any standard that you are held to as an expert in court that these women are suffering from post-traumatic stress syndrome?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, although I do acknowledge that VG-063 informs from records that she has been diagnosed elsewhere, but, no, not form -- I can't diagnose directly, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we will get into that because I think that that's -- well, okay. We'll get into that in a minute. But the fact that someone says they might be into psychiatric care, or may agree to a suggestion they have post-traumatic stress syndrome, you really can't draw any conclusions from that.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And obviously, you're not able to offer any scientific proof that any of these women are suffering from a disease that would give them a faulty memory?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And even if you did think, even if we did agree that they were suffering from PTSD, you still can't say whether they have a faulty memory?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I agree. It doesn't follow that even having that diagnosis necessarily means have you a faulty memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And PTSD, and I've learned a lot about that in the last couple of weeks, but it is a specific diagnosis of the DSM, the diagnosis book that doctors and psychologists and psychiatrists are held to in the US; right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: They are probably elsewhere. And there are specific symptoms of PTSD, and one is flash-backs; right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So the typical example we hear about is the person in the Vietnam war where they all of a sudden are in the middle of the room, they're doing nothing and then they get a flash-back of something that happened on the combat field.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. From the records that you reviewed of all these of these witnesses, did you see anything at all to indicate that any of these women had flashbacks?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. However, let me qualify the diagnostic issue, which is that flash-backs are, yes, typically observed but not always. There are a number of ways in which intrusive ideas or images can be experienced, but flash-backs is certainly common.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So for PTSD, have you to have something that we just talked about. There has to be an avoidance behavior, right, some time of avoidance behavior, a numbing, and there's other buzz words that are used in the diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So really, you can't -- from just looking at the statements and the testimony, you can't diagnose whether these women have any of these symptoms?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that there's no scientific proof that post-traumatic stress syndrome or trauma would cause a person to report facts inaccurately?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's nothing from that diagnosis to compel a claim that there would be inaccurate reports. It does happen, but it doesn't follow that if this diagnosis then automatically there will be inaccurate reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in fact -- and I'm going to talk about this in a few minutes, but there's a difference between the word inaccurate and inconsistencies; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. So if anything, that there's -- there are articles out there, and people have opined, that there might be some sort of association between severe trauma and inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But nothing that you know of in terms of measuring accuracy.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, other than general observations and statements, but in terms of true measurement, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And it's true that a particular person who has been diagnosed, for instance, with PTSD could have a perfectly normal memory.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now there are also -- you would agree that there's studies that show that some traumatised individuals often have an increase of information over time, increase of information over time, which could also explain for some further details given over time, such as rape victims?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes there is an increasion of new information that comes forward. What have you to be careful about, though, is the question becomes how accurate is that information, and have you to work very hard to corroborate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. And just so we're clear here, you're certainly not suggesting to this Court that persons who've been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress syndrome or severe trauma or have suffered trauma, would not be reliable witnesses in a court of law, and you're not suggesting that, are you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not making that categorical claim, that they cannot be used as witnesses. I do offer the caveat that it's a cautionary tale, that you need to be alert to the possibility that they can be -- it's more difficult to follow them, and you have to listen more carefully to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough. So I think we all know, and you would agree with me that when it comes to witness credibility issues and reliability, that is strictly for the judges or, in America, the juries.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's why they're trained to hear cases.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So I want to talk a little bit about inconsistencies because it actually is interesting, but people can describe events differently, right, using different words on different occasions, even non-traumatised people.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And -- so when telling a story differently, it doesn't mean that it false or inaccurate on any occasion.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in terms of consistency, doesn't consistency in answers depend on a lot of different factors, such as who's asking the questions, how the questions are asked, the typical setting, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are influencing factors, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And as long as the thread, I think was that the word you used, thread, yesterday?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thread. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: As long as the thread is consistent throughout the statement, then that is important, right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But the peripheral details, as they're referred to, can be different when different questions are asked. If a question is asked differently, the peripheral details might change --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: -- colour of eyes, colour of hair -- okay. In this particular -- in this context, we have, as you know, multiple statements from the witnesses, testimony from one to two different trials, and you have different people asking the questions, and you also have different interpreters, so you also have to factor in, don't you, that an interpreter may interpret something differently.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, we have had debates in this courtroom about interpretation problems. Even what we're staying gets misinterpreted on the record, and there has to be checks and corrections made. So if it happens here, it would happen out there when someone is being interviewed at their house, for instance.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It would also depend a lot on how the statement's being recorded, if someone's taking notes, if someone's writing down verbatim, someone is recording it, or someone is typing it, that would all make a difference in how the statement is written; right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And there also is the question about consistency and inconsistency. Something may not be an inconsistency at all. It just may be additional information. In other words, someone doesn't mention at one time that someone is present but mentions it another time, that is not necessarily an inconsistency, is it?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but it depends on the context in which the new information is being introduced. I think you do have to evaluate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, couldn't it also be, for instance, if I'm talking about 70 people in a room and I name everybody I can remember, but then the second time I'm asked by the person, Well, was so and so there? Would that jog my memory? Yes, that person was there. I didn't say it the first time because I can't remember 70 names, but I said it the second time because the person specifically asked me. So that can account for changes over time, can't it, different statements?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And that's not an inconsistency, sit?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, you talked about a lot of studies yesterday, just one little thing, you did not include all the studies you mentioned in your report of these three women. Did you know you didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the literature file?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in fact, most of them you didn't reference. When you talked about Kraft and Dember and Reuben [phoen] and all of the rest of them, there was no reference in your report to any of those. I was quite surprised yesterday when you mention those because they weren't in your report.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no reference to -- I want to track with you here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's missing?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No reference to the Robert Kraft study or William Dember study, Karen Nelson study -- you went down a litany of studies that you relied upon when writing your report, but we didn't know about those, so ...

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, they were listed in the folder with the various studies I looked at. I mean, I looked at those and others. Some of them I read but didn't necessarily incorporate into a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: With all of these studies that you've read, aren't there a lot of studies that show, in fact, that memory for the gist of an event is generally quite good, but it's the fuzzy details, the peripheral details that might be less clear.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Often that's the case, but it also depends on the way in which the memory was initially encoded. If it was encoded under high stress conditions, such as a traumatic event, then you would anticipate a different encoding process and a different retrieval process than you might anticipate under normal everyday circumstances. The anxiety can have its effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in terms of accuracy, Dr. Hough, isn't it almost impossible to test someone's memory for accuracy?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are memory tests, obviously, and you can assess various kinds of memory and get aggregate summations regarding people's memory capacity. In terms of memory accuracy, I'm not sure of a good way to do that, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right, and I think it's because -- I mean, for instance, take the Vietnam veteran's example's again because that is one example used. You can't test their memory because nobody was there.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. Okay. The same way we can't accurately test the memory -- you can't test the memory of traumatised victims for accuracy because you didn't go through the trauma. You weren't there.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So you're not able to -- no psychologist can offer an opinion about whether a particular individual is accurate in what they have reported?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. You can comment upon whether there's consistency across time and so on, but in terms of the accuracy of the recollection, that's an internal -- that's an internal world that I don't have access to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in terms of eye-witness accuracy, you'd agree with me, wouldn't you, that most of the studies with regard to eye-witness identification have all been about line-ups or photo spreads or that type of controlled study.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's most of it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. And they're usually studies of college students who are called in and have watched a film -- an incident on a film and they're asked to pick out someone from the line-up.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you know of any study where people were asked to recognise someone whom they'd known for years?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know of any research that suggests that people cannot recognise someone that they knew?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than if you looked at the -- say, the literature on Alzheimer's disease or something like that, where people sometimes forget loved ones, bout other than that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yeah. And I did miss one point that I wanted to follow up with regards to the studies with the college students watching. Again, those studies have to do with the ability or the inability of a person to identify a total stranger whom they saw in this video-clip. That's generally most of the studies, right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, okay, so they are not -- again, my follow-up was they're not asked in these studies to pick someone out of a line-up whom they knew on the film?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know of any research that suggests that trauma might interfere with the memory of someone to such a degree that a person could not recognise someone who they'd known for years?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that literature, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you're not aware of any -- excuse me. Now, I'm just curious, with regard to the three witnesses in this case, did you happen to count up the number of consistencies?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started to with VG-114, but then I decide I think I had enough. I don't remember how many I got.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think you -- maybe it's mistranslated. No. I know you did that with inconsistencies. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm talking about consistencies.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, consistencies, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So you don't know what the proportion was of the statements -- proportion of inconsistent versus consistent.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could it have been 10 per cent inconsistent, 90 per cent consistent?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without both counts, I wouldn't have a percentage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Would it be important, though, for your opinion, your analysis to study the consistencies?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could have been useful.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And also when you were looking at the materials, did you distinguish between -- you didn't distinguish, I imagine, between any peripheral details and those that are the thread details because you don't really know that much about the case, right? So you didn't distinguish about what is important and what isn't important?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Central versus peripheral, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Central versus peripheral. Okay. Also in regards to your evaluation and analysis, did you read any of the testimony of our other 40 witnesses to see if they corroborated any of the three witnesses?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't asked to review an extra 40 cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm sure you're busy. Would that have been helpful to see what other witnesses said and then to look at what these women said and put it into context? Would that be helpful?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose. If you were really going to go that far, it might have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What do you mean go that far?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would have been a lot of reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Right. But as you said yesterday, I think you started out --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. Just the problems with the speakers, and could they slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We have to slow down. What was my last ... Yeah, okay, did you read any other testimony -- right, you were busy. But yesterday -- I think you started out your testimony, there's a lot at stake here, and it's pretty -- this is -- there's a lot at stake.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. So in order to do a full and complete and proper analysis, you probably would need to look at some of the other evidence, the corroborating evidence.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To do it completely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, and also to examine the women.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Yourself. Okay. Now, when you were asked to do this, who asked you to review these? Was it Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And again, did he give you the materials? Did he say, Here's the transcripts and the statements, and ask you to do something with them?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He handed me the binders and said, I'd like you to review the materials and basically tell me what you think, and does it, in the vernacular, hang together?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you ask for any other materials in the course of your reviewing everything? Did you say -- if a witness -- one of the witnesses, for instance, referred to another witness, would you have wanted to read that witness's statements too?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to concentrate on VG-63 first, and I apologise here. I've mislaid ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If you want, we could bring up your report on the screen. This is VG-63. It was marked for identification. Do you have it -- thank you, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sure. 1D22-0788. And I apologise, I didn't have my microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you a couple of questions about, again, going back to inconsistencies. You made a -- you talked yesterday about her statements about the aggressor soldier carrying the head and the aggressor soldier and then again Milan Lukic. Again, you don't know whether this person -- how the questions were asked, and you don't know whether on the third occasion or the occasion where she was asked whether someone asked if it was Milan Lukic. You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So it may not be an inconsistency at all. Is that -- I mean, is it possible?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. It's unresolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. It's unresolved. Okay. Now, also, some of your -- what you consider to be inconsistencies are -- you refer to the witness being confronted, confronted by Mr. Cepic in particular. Well, you know that in a court, for instance, right now, here, I can put anything to you -- well, within reason.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. It doesn't mean it's true.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's true. That's a correct statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. So if a lawyer puts a proposition to a witness, it doesn't necessarily mean it's true.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But you rely on that when you say she's confronted with a fact, and you said she was confronted with the fact she placed Mr. Momir Savic at the Hasan Veletovac school at the time he had been in Slovenia. That's what Mr. Cepic said. That's not what the -- you don't know for sure whether that witness was in Slovenia, so you don't know whether that's an inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is a wrong interpretation, what I said in the transcript, what this expert quoted in his report. It was related -- my quotation in the transcript was related to the judgement in Mitar Vasiljevic case, not about some other things, and it was clearly quoted in this report as far as I understood. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Make sure you have it correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it was -- well, it's something that Dr. Hough quoted in his report, so if it's not accurate, then it just makes -- it's not -- should be taken out of the report or corrected, Your Honour. I don't know. I'm asking about it, and I assume it was done. It was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is really -- sometimes I'm -- Your Honour, with your leave, sometimes I'm really surprised with the allegations from opposite side. I think that the Prosecutor had enough time to check those allegations, to check the transcript, and to check the judgement from Vasiljevic case. It is quotation from the judgement related to that witness VG-115. Thank you very much. I apologise for disturbing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, all I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio, I would suggest that you move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But in drafting your report, though, you have to assume that everything you read is -- you assume it's correct.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed in that report, yes, that that statement was correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the tattoo issue, you said at one time, are you aware that this witness on two occasions in court twice said that she didn't see tattoos on Mr. Lukic, and she twice said she didn't remember saying that in a statement, so she has said that. So is it a possibility that the person who was taking the statement just wrote it down there wrong and ...

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, on page 2 of your report, and I know you have it in front of you, you talk about the combination of conditions and overall psychiatric status with her capacity to provide rational and consistent reports. Are you saying that someone that's suffered a traumatic event and maybe second trauma isn't rational or can't provide rational information?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not. What I'm alluding to is in this particular case of VG-063, we have a combination of sources of trauma. One would be the experiences of the war. The second would be that which she experiences in her own home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We have to - sorry - strike that, about ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you just avoid talking about any -- well, it's not really -- if we're going to talk about the personal details, we have to go into private session, so you can talk -- we know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session? No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No. I think we're okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I guess the point I would make would be that we have what would be considered a compounding of traumatogenic conditions from two different sources. And again, I cannot claim that even with the compounding that makes that, therefore, she can't provide testimony or rational testimony, but it does mean that the loading, the potential for that increases, and that I do think that we see at times a slippage in testimony, whether it's due to the convergence of these two types of trauma or some other source, I don't know, but we see that. So I note the trauma and the compounding trauma only as a factor to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you mentioned, also, in this report and in others, you talk about this -- the fact that the witnesses are under psychiatric care. Now, you would agree with me that -- you know, you're in the business, so someone being under psychiatric care doesn't make them any less accurate or any less reliable, does it?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not necessarily, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And also taking medication for some disorders isn't going to affect them in any way, memory or accuracy or ...

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the case, but by and large you can't make a general claim that because you're on medications or you're under care, that you are impaired, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in fact, you know, I think you'd agree with me that there are a lot of lawyers and doctors and other professionals who take medication for, say, depression, Prozac, on a daily basis, and they're carrying out their activities just fine.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And -- okay. Now I can move on to VG-114.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We can put that report up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, this is the woman Zehra who we contend is the sole survivor of a fire. Do you have it? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It was Y027-3870.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And I guess we'll start with the first page, the bottom of the first page. The bottom. Oh, is that the bottom? Okay, the top of the second page, then. It's the first paragraph of your report. You say that you found no evidence from any of the materials that you've reviewed that "a thorough forensic analysis was completed to determine the scope of the fire, the kinds of accelerants that may have been used, or the human remains that would have been left by such a fire." You say that; right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, why is that important an evaluation of a witness's testimony? In the context of this, why is that important?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would refer forward, I guess, to in my mind the unresolved question in terms of the statements, the claims, gas cylinder versus house fire. So I do think that helping resolving that question by forensic analysis at the site would be useful. And in many of the cases I work, I also review the forensic evidence that comes in regarding the crime scene itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you know these crimes occurred 16, 17 years ago.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you say "I find no evidence from any of the materials I have reviewed ..." Well, the only thing you were given to review were their statements, so why would anything about the forensic materials be in these witness statements and the transcripts?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I reviewed everything the attorneys gave me, and there was nothing of that nature in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It would have been helpful for you to have said, since I haven't reviewed anything else. You know, because you don't know -- because you haven't reviewed the whole thing, you don't know what forensic analysis was or was not done. So you can't make an assumption here that there was one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: For clarification, the witness asked me for police reports, and we were not able to give him something that would have complied with that in the true sense of the word that might have included such information, so we gave him what we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I understand that, but again, the report should be clear that you weren't provided with any police reports to draw any type of conclusion about what or wasn't done. Isn't that fair to say, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's probably fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk to you about Zehra's -- what happened to her in court. Are you aware that the reason she left court was because unannounced, without any notice, without any preparation as she's on the stand, she was shown photographs of herself all burnt that she hadn't seen for years.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon me. Can you tell me, was this the first time or the second time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The first time. That's why she had to leave and take a break. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. It assumes facts not in evidence, and the witness left the stand as we were going through photographs, and I don't think we were ever provided any particular information with regards to the situation, so I would say that it's an improper hypothetical and assumes facts not in evidence before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness did leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I know that, but I mean -- we were never -- one, I'm curious -- well, if the Prosecution was not able to have this particular contact and we weren't given any particular notice, I'm wondering how this particular theory as to why she left the stand is presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I mean, no one had contact with Zehra Turjacanin. I the it was very clear what happened. Mr. Cepic called up the video of her first interview, and when it was put on the screen in front of her, an image she had not seen for 17 years, an image showing her terribly injured, she just immediately said, Please, I need to leave the courtroom. And she was escorted out of the courtroom, so it doesn't take any interview. I think it's a reasonable deduction we can all make. We were all here. We witnessed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the question is what --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The question is basically would that have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If it is put that way --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. If it is put the way that Mr. Groome just put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If that were the case, would that be important for you to know that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Let me say several things. First of all, I didn't know what the stimuli that she was reacting to was until just now; but second, yes, it would be important because it would suggest to me as a clinician that she is responding to -- she's being overstimulated by something. We call it a trigger. She has been triggered by having seen these pictures that she has not seen for these many years that reminds her of the trauma. That trigger kind of reaction, trigger phenomena is often what we see in the traumatic conditions, so it would have been clinically useful, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But it could also happen to a normal person who sees something that horrifying. Have you seen the pictures of her?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw a video-clip, but -- I think I saw that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: As I said, a normal person could also have this -- not a normal person. Someone not suffering from a disorder could also have this reaction.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially if it's a picture of themselves in that condition. That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to clarify that on September 25th; 2008, the witness left the stand during my cross-examination and not during Mr. Cepic's presentation. I believe Mr. Cepic had the opportunity to cross-examine during the return of Ms. Turjacanin, which happened -- yeah, sometime -- considerable -- and on November 4th is when she was shown this, and for what context that is in, that's not the reason why she left and did not return until November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And also in your report of VG-14, yes, you make note of the fact that she asked -- she told the officer -- she told them about the burns being the result of another accident. Now, you know having been in the Balkans and seeing the war and what it's done to people that someone who is a Bosnian Muslim civilian woman going to the Serb police and telling them that something had happened and done by Serbs, probably wouldn't have been a smart thing to do, would it, for her?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean to tell them about a fire? Is that what you're --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, telling them that Milan and Sredoje Lukic set fire to the house.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may not have been. I don't know enough about the circumstances to say that with certainty, but, you know, that's possible that that could have been in her appraisal, in her analysis of what to say. That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So all of these different things that I'm pointing now --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This witness never said that my client set the fire in that house, so this is -- I don't see any foundation for those kind of allegations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm asking him about the report to the police department, not -- it's a hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is unacceptable, completely unacceptable from my point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, sir, other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Other witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you're going to rely on the evidence, you have to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: There is no such report. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: There isn't, but other witnesses, particularly VG-119 has said that this witness told her that, so there is evidence, and I don't think we should be arguing about the evidence in front of the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And also -- I apologise. May I -- Your Honour, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio, how much longer will you be?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll move on very quickly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for disturbing, and just for the record, this witness never said this, she went to the police and report. Thank you very much, and I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just a few more questions about this witness. It's important, isn't it, Doctor, when you write a report that you do provide citations for everything you cite to, and I know you tried to do that in this report, but there are a lot of sentences that don't have any citations.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's true. I mean, I cited the ones that I thought were important, but I suppose an argument can be made that every sentence should be cited.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. Because otherwise we don't -- when you say -- you talk about in the third paragraph on page 4 - page 4, please, thank you - the last paragraph, when you talk about on cross-examination, you say, for example, in earlier versions of her narrative she said her brother and Mr. Lukic were close friends, now she does not. You don't cite anything there, so can you explain why each one of your facts is not cited?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May we now have the letter regarding VG-115, which is Y027-3879.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this, you say: "Turning to the documents, it becomes evident that witness VG-115 has serious emotional problems." You conclude that.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you show me where you are again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It's the first paragraph of the report: "I begin this analysis ..." and it's toward the end. Turning to the documents, it becomes evident that VG has serious emotional problems. Can you tell that somebody has serious emotional problems just by looking at a document, or should you be doing that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is document analysis, and you -- I mean, I haven't provided a technical diagnosis, but I have alluded to a number of ways in which I infer from the material that there are some problems here, so I think that's a fair -- it's a summary statement and later on in the report I go on to flesh that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But you also rely with regard to this witness on the fact that she says, and you quote her, I was out of my mind, that if it wasn't for my daughter, I would have killed myself. Now, don't you consider that to be actually a rational thought, that she didn't consider it because of her daughter?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part is -- the statement as a whole is both rational and irrational. The irrational part is -- well, I don't know if it's irrational, but she's telling us how desperate she had become, that she had been pushed to the brink of contemplating taking her own life. The rational part is that she can step back and observe and recognise that she does have something to live for: Her daughter. That becomes a protective factor, a buffer against action.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It could also be interpreted that she's responsible, that she's living up to her responsibilities as a mother.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's true too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That has my point, though. You can look at any number of these factors that you've cited to, and there is more than one way of looking at the conclusions that you've drawn and the citations. For instance, you mentioned further on on page 2, you mentioned about the transportation, the ride home. When confronted about accepting a ride from Mr. Slobodan Roncevic from her place of employment to her home, her answer confuses the concept of accepting a ride home for transportation, with the sexual connotation of being taken home. But, again, you don't know in a different culture when someone says, I'm going to take you home, that's what they mean. We can't rule that out.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. But that was my read on it, but I agree with your point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Thanks. Now, another point which is further up when you talk about Mitar Vasiljevic, she responded when asked where he was to locate a mark on the scene, she responded, Do you think he just stood in a single spot? And for some reason you said her thinking could not flexibly allow for representation on a map to represent more than him. Well, actually, I thought -- can't you read that as she's being actually very astute? She's telling the person, the Prosecutor, or whoever's asking her, he didn't just stand in one spot, so I can't just put one spot. She's actually doing a better job of answering the question than was asked of her.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could, but I think the general task was to -- that the X on the -- the indicator, the spot on the map would be a generalized representation of where he was. And to try to -- for her to specify that he moved around a lot is -- it's a bit of a concretization. It's not serious, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the Vasiljevic judgement, which has been referred to, alluded to in your testimony yesterday, you didn't read the judgement, did you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was referencing the commentary from Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Cepic. I know. It's hard to pronounce. Have you to be here a while to --

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So you we are referencing again his comment about it. You don't know if that's true.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- no, you're right. I haven't read the judgement, but I have no reason to believe that an officer of the court in open court would make a false claim deliberately, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But there are many reasons why a witness may not be found credible in another case and found credible in another case; isn't that true? There's different circumstances, different witnesses in the cases. They're two separate cases, so you can't carry one into the other based on a question by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It violates the principles of res judicata and calls for the witness to make a legal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Not res judicata, but move on. I don't think there is much point in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Law of the case, Your Honour. A pre-adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, you don't know the circumstances of that case, do you?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you don't know exactly what the judges said in the judgement?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you did rely on that. You did put that in your report without really knowing the full stance circumstances; right?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I have one moment, Your Honour, and I may be finished. I have no further questions of Dr. Hough. Thank you, Dr. Hough, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long will you be? Is there another witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Not too long, and we are prepared Ms. O'Leary and Mr. Jenkins are en route only because they are offline, or Ms. O'Leary is offline, rather. So actually I expected this to go to full session, but it's not, so we would be ready at least to start Mr. Jenkins, I'm assuming. If we could -- I'll probably know either if she pops up on the screen, which sometimes happens, and/or at the break might be a good opportunity, and Mr. Ivetic can go out and check right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic, please go and check and bring her in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what's this document, Your Honour, the power of attorney we're going to have to execute before we start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a standard document with the Registry. They'll tell you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I just want to facilitate that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, let's start first with going back through, and we'll just do it in the order of the cross-examination. You know, obviously -- well, you indicated in your report that some of the sources you looked at were newspaper articles and general news and/or reporting, as well as you probably looked at the web site here, case information sheet, the indictment as some due diligence before you got involved?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why would you be looking for psychopathy when looking at this kind of case? You said that you were half-surprised or whatnot as to what you were looking for.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would be looking for psychopathy because in a case where someone had actually engaged in the actions for which this defendant has been accused, that this is the kind of behavior that one would fully anticipate from somebody who is of a psychopathic nature, and by that I mean specifically is able to kill without remorse, lacks conscience, and doesn't see the value in human life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that some issues might start showing up as a juvenile, and you used the reference point of a teenager. What kind of things would you expect, and why is that important?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Typically, the budding psychopath would begin to manifest in adolescence, typically manifested by, say, getting in trouble with the law, engaging in miscreant behaviors that bring that child to the attention of the law, so juvenile delinquency. Often you will see school problems or school failure, moving into a deviant lifestyle characterized by heavy use of drugs or alcohol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. And also you considered you were questioned a little bit about the basic overall intelligence, average, below average, whatnot. Why is that important for your analysis?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because generally speaking, the higher the intelligence, the more capable that individual really is of functioning in the world. Someone of very low intelligence would not be expected to function as well or as adaptively as someone with very high intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to pose this as a hypothetical, but I would proffer that some evidence was given in this case by a witness or witnesses actually that knew him in the general area of his high school years. And one witness, in fact the witness that accuses him of trying to shoot him at the Drina River says that Milan Lukic did not fight or get in fights and hadn't been aggressive as far as he knew. How does that play into your -- how would that fact -- if it were shown from a direct witness, how would that factor in? Would that be a collateral source, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is outside the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it outside the scope, Your Honour? I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I rule it's outside. It doesn't arise. Don't redo the evidence that you led in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would you expect to find someone of this -- of emerging psychopathic tendencies to have violent or aggressive behavior early on?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, VG --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We've been through that already. We've been through that already. Let's move on and conclude this gentleman's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I can't remember if I gave you VG-63's testimony, but if I were to proffer to you that she said she knew him in school and that he was always trying to be the centre of attention -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That she was always try to be the centre of attention but he need to be helped in school, would that be a collateral source for purposes of your evaluation?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would in terms of functioning in an educational environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you were cross-examined on lack of collateral sources. In an ideal set of circumstances, would you would have to complete your evaluation in so few hours?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you say that again for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Under ideal situations -- I mean, in this situation there were timetables and obviously access, you know, problems considering where you're at and where him and his family are at. But under normal circumstances, would you take much more time to do those collateral sources and follow-up?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. The logistics here are just so complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, Judge David posed some questions to you about Binswanger, and I'd like you to explain to the Court the circumstances where the -- someone would be governed more by the societal pushes or the authority that may be pushing, and I'd like you to explain in a very brief nutshell for the Court the Milgram studies.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have referenced the Milgram studies as representative or, rather, as a paradigm, an explanatory concept to try to explain why it would be that many individuals under certain environmental circumstances engage in behaviors for which they would not otherwise have engaged had they not been in that circumstance.
