And Milgram is one of the paradigmatic lines of study that approach that problem. He engaged in a series of experiments at Yale University, over 20 variations, looking at the problem of obedience to authority. Milgram had been very concerned about how could it be from World War II that so many people had seemingly followed blindly. In a nutshell, what he's able to demonstrate in his study is that human beings do have a powerful propensity to obey authority, and he showed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Your follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think it's a powerful analogy to briefly go through the circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want to hear anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I think we all know about the Milgram experiments. It's very common knowledge to professionals like you, but you're not talking to a jury, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's fair enough. To be honest, I hadn't heard of Milgram until Dr. Hough told me about it, and so I wouldn't presume that you would have exposure, although I would presume because you're here, of course, I'm sure the defence has been raised before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, there was some concern posed by the Prosecution that all the information is coming from him. But how do you take that into account -- I mean, I'm sure you have to consider that in a forensic evaluation regardless of the access to collateral sources, and tell us how you balance that.

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, this is a case where I did have to rely so far primarily upon the self-report from the man examined himself. In an ideal situation, of course, I would have tried to have gathered as much collateral information as possible. But short of that looking at his own self-report, I look at internal consistency. I look for the way in which he tells his narrative. I look for the way in which he's related to me in terms of the patient-examining relationship. I look for contradictions, gaping omissions. I look for times when he becomes emotionally pressured or not. I look for a lot of clinical indicators that are ongoing and constantly being monitored in the process of the evaluation. So there is a clinical diagnostic process unfolding at every moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what do you factor in as your inability to have access to the subject, and what normally do you do in terms of revisiting this with the accused?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I try to get as much extra collateral as I can when I can get it, but beyond that I would go back and try to revisit with the accused and go over those particular areas that remain unresolved or which I have specific concerns about. And I would always as much as I can try to get into the details themselves about the allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, there was some reference to -- and brought up -- it was admitted as P -- I believe it was 313.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could we have that, page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just as a lead-up while they're putting it on the screen, there was a discussion between you and the Prosecutor regarding his role in the military and the command structure. But specifically, he referred to a commander, Vinko Pandurevic, simply as in the chain of command above him. How -- did you assess him as being in a paramilitary or in the military based on that reported information?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, he told me a number of times in many ways that he was in the command structure of the military, but that particular name, General Pandurevic, in my understanding would clearly implicate him as being in the chain of command, and he denies having ever been outside that chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: A moment, Your Honour. I'm just reviewing my notes. I don't have much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What other factors -- with regards to -- let's move on to the witnesses, please. Talking generally with regards to the women witnesses that were referenced in your letter reports, the Prosecution brought up certain issues about these -- or actually, I think you brought it up, that statement-taking procedures, the differences between them can account for some of the inconsistencies, yet can there be a complication from the test-taking procedures that would also affect the reliability of those statements, or do you have a feeling on that?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I feel like you're asking me several questions here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I probably am. How important is consistency in the statement-taking procedures?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Consistency in that methodology is important, I would say very important. Ideally, the statements would be gathered by the same individual across time. Then you would have a control on that consistency question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, statistically speaking or within your experience, does memory become clearer over time?

utterances.speaker: GEORGE HOUGH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general consensus --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This was all covered in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. You're just rehashing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to cut it way down, but these were brought up in cross-examination, so I at least believe this is proper subject matter. If the Court feels I've adequately covered the issues on direct, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will pass the witness. And simply as a matter of housekeeping, I would introduce the exhibits into evidence for the weight to be assessed by the Court, but I think the relevance and the expertise have been established, and I would like to list them in individually. I believe the CV has already been admitted, 1D22-0719. I would tender the evaluation of Milan Lukic, 1D22-0735. I would tender the analysis of Witness VG-115 as 1D22-0775. I would tender the analysis of VG-114, which is 1D22-0779. And I would tender the appendix to said analysis as 1D22-0784. And I would tender the analysis of Witness VG-63, 1D22-0788. I would tender those into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would have something -- we would like to speak to that but not in front of the witness. May the witness be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You want to speak to what? The admission of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, why should the witness be excused? He has completed his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As a matter of fact -- you have finished your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. We can do this. Witness, that concludes your evidence. I thank you for giving it and particularly for the frank manner in which you have given it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I think it would be appropriate that if you consider the exhibits, they should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the Prosecution's position that these -- the report and the three letters should not be admitted. There's really hardly any indicia of reliability whatsoever to these documents. I mean, the doctor is a professional, and he did what he could, but all we have is a self-report of Milan Lukic. It's Milan Lukic's statement to the Court without having to take the stand. That's all it is, and he admitted that, and he admitted the short-comings in that report, so it really cannot have no value. And it shouldn't be admitted and considered as evidence in this case. And with regard to the witnesses, Your Honour, he admitted the short-comings there. He did not see these women. He doesn't know. And all he can say is, you know, people with trauma may have difficulty recording things. And I think that, again, these should not be admitted in evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I disagree with you strongly. It only goes to weight. I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit the report by majority, Judge Van Den Wyngaert dissenting.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D22-0375 will become Exhibit 1D203. 1D22-0775 will become Exhibit 1D204. 1D22-0779 will become Exhibit 1D205. 1D22-0784 will become Exhibit 1D206. And 1D22-0788 will become Exhibit 1D207. All are placed under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic. It appears that a question has been raised about the propriety of Ms. O'Leary doing the examination. I am told that in the Milutinovic case, the person involved was in fact assigned to the Milutinovic case. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. In both instances, they were assigned to the case as Ms. O'Leary is so assigned on our case, I believe. We've never --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: As far as the Registry was concerned, Your Honour, we never made a formal request for her to be removed. We picked up our new case manager, of course, because she wasn't able to take on the lion's share of the duties, but in a ghost-writing perspective or at least some help in assisting us to show us where things are going, she helps us all the time, and she's been a wonderful asset. So I think for practical purposes she's part of our family on this team, and we consider her as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that to be an obstacle, that she's not assigned to the case. It distinguishes it from Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my position was there would be nothing from a rules perspective, I would hope, that would prevent a licensed attorney from taking a particular witness if -- you know, I think it's a good opportunity, but I wasn't aware there would be any actual impediment within the rules that was so specific. I mean, we could take the break and try to get in touch with Ms. Osure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now and see whether it can be ironed out. I'm not certain whether that obstacle can be gotten over, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not given to these -- interpreting rules in these rigid ways myself, but if they're there, then we may have to follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, let me speak first. I say, Mr. Alarid, I'm sorry that I have to disappoint Ms. O'Leary. OLAD has taken a point that she has not been assigned to this case. That's different from the Milutinovic case, and it would not be proper for her to appear as counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, over the break I resolved the matter and spoke personally with (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: the solution was found is to re-classify Ms. O'Leary as a pro bono legal assistant to signed. No new confidentiality materials need to be signed because they are already in the possession of OLAD, and she was simply going to get confirmation that Mr. Djordjevic of the Djordjevic Defence did not object. And she has a voice mail on her mailbox, and I have informed her of that from Mr. Djordjevic that there's no problem bauds Ms. O'Leary had of course had obtained prior approval from her lead counsel on that case to take the time off to take this witness. So from that stand point, I consider the matter resolved from the Registry side of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I congratulate you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I mean, but of course -- you're right. Making no assumptions, Your Honour, as to the issues that the Court make take with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Alarid, you seem to have resolved the situation, and I think you are to be complimented. We welcome Ms. O'Leary to the trial, and before the witness is called, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon. The Defence has provided us with a list of exhibits they intend to use through Mr. Jenkins, and on the list is something listed as a statement of Uscumlic, and then it says from 65 ter. Now, a very careful look at the 65 ter list does not reveal any statement from Zoran Uscumlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can clarify that, maybe. There's a similar name -- we should probably by in private session for this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while wire waiting for the witness to come in, Mr. Alarid made mention that there might be two of the subpoenaed witnesses appearing next week. The Prosecution would appreciate knowing which two so we can conduct our preparations over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have sent an e-mail to Mr. Stevan Cole of the Office of the Prosecutor listing the potential witnesses for next week. The first two on that list are the subpoena witnesses for whom we have received verification that they've been served.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Cliff Jenkins, Your Honour, and I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, and you may begin, Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: As you know, my name is Marie O'Leary, and I'm an attorney appearing on behalf of Milan Lukic. With me today is lead counsel for Mr. Milan Lukic, Mr. Jason Alarid, and co-counsel, Mr. Dragan Ivetic. Before we begin, I would like to remind you that because we are both seeking the same language, we should mind a pause between question and answer to make sure that there is enough time for translation. At the same time, be sure to speak slowly and clearly so that everything can be picked up for the record.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Yes, counsellor.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Could you please state your name for the record and spell.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: My name is Cliff Jenkins, C-l-i-f-f, J-e-n-k-i-n-s.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I live in Albuquerque, New Mexico. Would you like me to spell that for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: It's A-l-b-u-q-u-e-r-q-u-e.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: In Albuquerque.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And when were you are born?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: July 4th, 1950.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And are you married?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I do. I have two biological children. My family's a product of a blended family, so I have two biological children, three daughters that were adopted. I have a step-daughter and a step-son.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you give us a brief history of your education.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I am a product of public schools in the city of Albuquerque; graduated high school in 1968; enlisted in the Air Force in 1969 and the International Guard. When I returned from basic training, I then enrolled at the University of Albuquerque, completed three years with University of Albuquerque, and because of my job requirements, at that point was unable to finish my education at that point in time, and periodically over the years, went back, took classes, but never completed my formal degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And what position do you hold now?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I am the managing partner of a company could Jenkins & Jenkins LLC. We are -- we provide several different services to the legal community throughout the United States. Some of the things we do are similar to this in that we review cases and make recommendations to our clients on possible legal action. We also do things like mock jury scenarios where attorneys get a chance to make their arguments before a panel of citizens before they take their cases to court so that they can refine their arguments. We have been involved in a large environmental contamination case in Colorado and in New Mexico. We have done multiple what in the United States we term internal affairs investigations. That is investigations involving police misconduct. And the police organizations are too small to have a dedicated unit to perform those investigations, and they have come to us and contracted with our company to perform those investigations for them and report our findings to the chief or the mayor of that municipality so they can take appropriate disciplinary action if it's required.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And when was that company founded?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: That company was founded in January of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And who founded this company?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen, please, 1D22-0692.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, can you tell us, what's the last position that you held prior to founding that company?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I was the executive deputy chief of police for the city of Albuquerque, and effectively that is the second in command of the organisation, approximately 250 civilians employees, and at the time, right at that time 750 sworn officers. Could be a few more about that -- actually, as I think about it at the time I retired we were close to a thousand, 950 officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what tasks were in your responsibility when you were in that position as deputy chief?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Part of my responsibility, I really was in charge of everything that really didn't deal either with the field, with the officers that take calls for service or with investigations, with the detectives. But I was responsible for some investigative functions within the organisation: Internal affairs, audits, and inspections are all investigative functions within the department, but we also had responsibility for payroll, personnel, communications, our information systems developing, crime analysis, vehicle maintenance, the police academy, recruiting, all aspects of the police function outside of law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. There's a document on your screen now in front of you. Can you tell me what this document is.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: This is a copy of my CV.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about your experiencers then, if we go to page 2, and start with your work as a police officer. Just briefly, what duties did you undertake as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Well, in our organisation, you really start from the ground up. Everyone that's brought into the organisation begins as a patrolman second class. That is a period of time when you're on probation, and as you work your way up, there's a possibility to grow -- to grow your career. From the time I graduated from the police academy initially as all officers are, they're assigned to field services, which is the part of the department that takes calls for service; they write reports, conduct very preliminary investigations and then forward those reports in through the organisation. We also make misdemeanor arrests, DWIs, write traffic tickets, that sort of thing. In October of -- actually, I graduated from the police academy in December, end of December, 1st of January of 1972, going into 1973. Spent some time, approximately a little over a year, year and a half in the field. In October, I put a letter of request for transfer into the traffic division and was accepted, so I became a motorcycle police officer, and that's where I also began to hone some skills as an investigator investigating traffic accidents, traffic fatalities, as well as continuing to write citations, and make arrests for driving under the influence. Continued that process, was eventually accepted into what is called the field investigator programme. As a field investigator, you're responsible for the collection of evidence, handling of that evidence, making sure that it gets to the forensics departments properly sealed and maintained. We photograph crime scenes, all sorts of things that would not -- the lesser crimes that would not involve actually bringing a forensics team out to the field to investigate, the lower-level types of crimes; burglaries, robberies, some sex offenses, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you got involved in more investigative work or your investigative background.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I was selected to go to the burglary/narcotics unit after my stint in the field, and once I got into that unit, that is investigations per se. I mean, that is all you do is investigations, and I managed a caseload of approximately 35 to 40 cases a month that involved property crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what experience do you have in supervising investigations?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: When I was promoted to the rank of sergeant, my initial assignment was to the field, back into field services. After one year's time, I was then reassigned back into investigations to the crime lab. Because of my experience as a field investigator, they felt that I was in the best position to manage that team, and the crime scene team is the team that actually rolls out to major crimes like homicides, you know, if there is a big crime scene that is very technical in the way that it is approached and developed, so I was responsible for all of those sorts of investigations in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us a little bit further about homicide investigations that you worked on.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the homicide investigations that I worked in the laboratory, at the same time I was assigned in criminalistics or in the lab, I had tested for promotion to the rank of lieutenant and made the list for promotion, finished second on that list, so the commander of the investigations bureau asked if he could move me, then, from the lab to violent crimes until such time that I was going to be promoted. They want to get somebody in my position and start training them right away to get them up to speed. So I was -- I agreed to the transfer. They moved me then to violent crimes, and in violent crimes I oversaw the sex crimes unit, but we rotated through. There were three sergeants in that unit, the homicide sergeant, sex crimes, and robbery, and we rotated on an on-call basis, and as a result I managed to supervise the investigation, probably 35 homicides or so, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And can you tell us about any prior experience you have in testifying before a Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Before a Chamber such as this, I have no experience at all, but I have countless hours of testimony before US district courts at all levels, federal, state, and municipal courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what else in your expertise or included in your CV that we haven't touched upon do you feel helps the Trial Chamber assess your expertise?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I think just from that it's also important to note that I also had the opportunity to investigate very complex crimes in the organised crimes unit. Very -- in fact, international, there were a couple of international crimes that were investigated involving money laundering. And it's also important, I think, that the Tribunal know that I also have managed to climb through the ranks to -- finally to the rank of deputy chief and still maintained expertise in case review.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd move to admit Mr. Jenkins's CV.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object. And if the Chamber allows, I'd like to ask Mr. Jenkins a few questions about his expertise.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: We have no problem with it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have already admitted Mr. Jenkins as an expert. I know over the past week we had allowed certain questions, but the Chamber is not going to allow it on this occasion. You can ask your questions of him in cross-examination going to the weight of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So I would again move to admit the CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D208, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jenkins, how did you become involved in the present case?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I received a telephone call from the firm that Mr. Alarid is involved in asking me if I would be interested in reviewing the case with him when he was in town on a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: When did he first contact you?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I believe the first contact I had on the case from his colleague was -- I want to say around March of 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: March of 2008?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: When did he subsequently contact you?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: We finally met, if I remember right, the end of June of 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And as any preliminary matter, what process did you have to go through to become assigned to this case?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: There was a submission of my CV to the Registry, and at that point I guess it was reviewed by -- I'm really not familiar with the process on this end of it, but I assume that the CV was presented to whoever. The CV was accepted, and I received notification from the Registry that I had been accepted as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when that was? If you don't know, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you subsequently meet with Mr. Alarid to discuss the case further?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: We met in November of 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what was the proposed scope of your assignment?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: He asked me to review some specific areas, the Varda factory, the fire at the Bikavac scene and the Pionirska scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what qualifications do you have that make you suitable for such an assignment?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Just 30 years worth of good, hard police work and investigative experience as reflected in my CV and the ability to know and understand police functions, how they're supposed to function, and apply that in a -- I think, a fair and even-handed manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Now, I believe you've seen a copy of the indictment in this case.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why was your assignment limited to those incidents that you've listed, Pionirska, Bikavac, and Varda factory?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I think that's where my area of expertise really lies is in the crime scene evaluation of the process, not so much some of the outlying or peripheral items that are contained in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what perspective or goal did you have in the process of looking at the materials?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: My goal was simply to evaluate the process and whether or not it met the accepted standards for police investigations that are -- that were in affect not only now but also back in 1994 during the time that this incident took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- I think you said it was November. Can you tell us back in November, how did you go about beginning to review the materials?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I didn't review any of the materials until we had been accepted by the Registry. That was sometime after the initial meeting, and I -- as I said before, I couldn't tell you the exact date, but once that was done and the letter of confidentiality was executed, the materials were turned over to me for review. That included witness statements, and primarily that's it. I mean, there were no other reports or documents to review or to support.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Did you receive any subsequent materials, photos, other exhibits?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I have received photographs of the scenes that were, I guess, provided by the ICTY. We have copies of, like I say, the statements that were taken by the investigators for ICTY. That's really all the material I had at the beginning to review.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: But may I say, it was very voluminous. There was a lot of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I pause, it's simply for the translation. We'll discuss more later, but briefly, can you tell us if you performed any site visits?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: When did you perform site visits?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: In January of 2009, the end of -- January 29th, I believe, of 2009.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And if we could have 1D22-0696 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, there's a document in front of you on the screen. Can you tell us from the first page here, anyway, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: This is a copy of the report that I generated to the Registry concerning our site visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, I'd like to give the witness a hard copy so it's easier to flip through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page, please, and go down to the bottom of the page, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And whose signature is that on the last page?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: This is a facsimile of my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: But this is your report?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: This is my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: The same submitted?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Having had some time now to review this report in preparation for testimony, would there be any changes that you would make to this report?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Yes. There are specifically two items that I would amend.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start with the first one. What is the first change you would like the make?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: The first thing I would like to -- give me one second, and I'll give you the exact location. On page 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 7, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On paragraph 7, at the bottom it states that the bridge is not lighted, but in fact the bridge is lighted. I would like to amend that part of the report. The bridge is lighted.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said there was a second change you would like to make. What is the second change?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Second change, is also on page 7, that would be in paragraph 6, the one immediately preceding, and it deals with the damage to the eaves of the house. Since review of photographs since that time, I have determined that that roof was actually rebuilt at some point in time, so that would be why there would be no obvious fire damage to the eaves of that adjacent residence.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. We can call that up at another time later on in your testimony and discuss further, but thank you for noting that. If we could go in the report to page 3 now. And right about in the middle of the page. You indicate that you have some issues of concern, I believe you said. Can you please explain -- I don't want to get too ahead of ourselves, but if you could give us a brief overview of general concerns that you had.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: The issues of concern that I had concerning my review of the report are really -- for lack of a better word, I guess they are things that one would expect as a professional investigator, areas that should have been covered, and in my review they were areas that seemed to be lacking. So if there were some way that through further evidence being presented to the contrary, I would be glad to review any of that material, but at this point in time I have not seen anything that would change the way the report reads. I have major concerns with the way the entire investigation was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us, though, what those major concerns were?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Well, from the very onset the way that the witnesses were -- the way the statements were taken from the witnesses at the time. There's no memorialisation of those statements. They appear to be versions that the investigators -- they interviewed the witnesses. They then, for lack of better words, digested that information from the witnesses, and then had the statements drafted using the words of the investigator rather than the words of the witness themselves. By doing that, you run the risk of -- I won't say contaminating; that's not necessarily the case, but you run the risk of injecting your own bias as an investigator into the investigation. And it also causes problems because there's no accurate record of what the witnesses have truly said. It's certainly possible that because of questions of dialect, of regional slang or whatever that the words of the witness possibly could have been misunderstood, and there's no way to go back and know for sure exactly what the witness said. And some of those things are critical to this particular investigation because it deals so much with the nuances of the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: I want to go back to your first concern here because it is your first concern in the report, where you're speaking about witness credibility. And you list a series of questions at page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4, please, and skip right down to number 6, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: You were briefly just discussing this, but what are these questions that you've listed here? What do these questions represent?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Well, they represent a standard by which investigators should be conducting themselves when they're interviewing witnesses, the idea being that you do not want to lead the witness to a conclusion that you want them to make. I want to know what the witness is saying without necessarily any interpretation, so I think the proper way in this case to conduct these investigations would be to ask open-ended questions that would give the witness the opportunity to tell their story with as little interruption as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And how can translation affect statement-taking?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Well, it's a tremendous problem, I think, in a lot of areas where you're dealing with people that have -- they're using two or three languages. For example, if the investigators are using English and the witnesses are speaking Bosnian or Serbian, whichever, there's a bridge that has to be built by the question that's being asked on one side; it goes through the bridge to the Bosnian side. We get a response to the question, and then it comes back the other way. Well, if there's a misinterpretation or a misunderstanding of the question, then all of a sudden it generates issues within the investigation as to whether or not it was accurately translated, and the correct nuances were asked of the individual. The only way to get around that that I can see is if it is a recorded -- a continuously recorded statement, much like the transcript of a trial, so that the investigator will have the opportunity to at a later time go through the recording or go through the transcript line by line and make sure that there are no issues. And also by doing that, it saves the record so that at a later time Defence can independently have the tape transcribed and also for the Prosecution, you can look at those translations side by side to make sure that there are no glaring errors in the way the questions are asked or in the answers that are received.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What observations did you make about this statement-taking method used in this case?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: The method, although it may be acceptable in some sorts of investigations, for example, a white collar crimes case where most of the evidence that's going to be reviewed really deals with documents and the documents will speak for themselves, this particular investigation or this type of a case involves an accused perpetrator. This is a different type of investigation than a white collar investigation. The nuances are much more important. The credibility of the witnesses are much more important, and therefore, they should be examined more closely.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What effects would in statement-taking process have on a direct commission case such as this, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Well, it really provides the first level of the investigative process, so as an investigator, what I want to do is I want to take the statements that my witnesses have given me, and based on that I'm looking for a foundation and direction on how I want to approach this case. So the statements of the witnesses will help me determine which way the investigation is -- what turns it's going to take to completion, and it's important especially in those early statements that as much information -- truthful and accurate information as possible be gained because from that information, we will develop suspects; we will develop an investigative plan on how we want to approach the crime scene; and really, it is -- those initial statements are the foundation from which the rest of the building blocks of the case will be built.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: In looking also at your report, if we move up to number 3, you ask the question: "Is the witness associated with any victim rights groups that have other agendas?" What specific concerns arise out of that, or why would an investigator ask that question?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: I think it speaks to motive. I think it speaks to credibility. If there is a victims rights group involved in the process, especially later on, it calls into question the entire reason why in person is coming forward. Is this person -- and it's simply a question that you as an investigator have to ask yourself: Why is this person coming forward? Is the person coming forward in order to receive reparation? Is there some reward or benefit to this individual for coming forward? And if so, if you can make that determination, what is the witness saying? Is it of value to me? Do I get some sort of gain by bringing this information forward? I mean, it just really speaks to the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: You talk about motives for providing false information. Have you experienced in your own time as a police officer people with motives?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How does an investigator ferret out false motives, false testimony motives?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Well, it's important, I think, to understand the nature of the crime. You know, are there any family ties associated with this crime? Revenge is a tremendous motive; so is finances. They're tremendous motives. Did the individual come forward of their own volition and provide information? Are they trying to support the contentions of another family member who has already given a statement? Are there religious ties associated? I mean, you really have to look at all of the aspects of someone that has an association with some sort of a victims rights group and ask, you know, is the information valid? And I'm not saying you should totally discount what they have to say. But what I am saying is that you need to look at the motive and be satisfied yourself that the information that they're giving you is true and correct and not motivated by some other factor.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What type of flexibility does an investigator have to have, then, to try to understand the person they're interviewing and determine whether there is some albeit mistaken or intentional false testimony?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Well, I think you have a great deal, and what you have to do is you have to look at statements of the other witnesses. Does the information this witness is giving you, is it in lock-step with information from other witnesses? The way you can -- the way you can separate out -- the way you can separate out the information is by -- I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps just as well. Ms. O'Leary, it seems to me that we have covered the general principles of proper investigation, and what we now should be doing is applying them to the case because I presume that he has specific comments to make about the case, which can assist us in our work here.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: You've heard the Judge's comments. In applying it to the statements that you viewed to the ICTY, what possible motive, accidental, intentional, what factors went into specifically statement-taking here that could affect any sort of credibility in this specific situation in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: We don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Because there are no reports that have been filed by the investigators, so we have no way of knowing what processes were taken in order to collect those statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: In this Tribunal, there's a lot of media coverage because of the large scale of it. How can that affect the statements of the witnesses taken in these cases?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Well, assuming that these people have to go home if they're still living in the Visegrad area or, for that matter -- it doesn't really matter. I mean, if they're going back into their civilian lives, there is the potential for tremendous pressure being applied to them by groups of individuals of their own ethnicity that would like to see an outcome that is favorable to their point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And I think we can move on now from the statement-taking and move on to the area of forensics, which I know you dealt a good deal with in your report, I believe if we turn to the next page of the report. On page 5, you mention a listing of failures of field investigators in the forensics process. If we go one by one, what can you tell me about the forensics that were done? What reports did you review in Pionirska?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: First of all, may I just say that the crimes that are being heard by the Tribunal are certainly horrific, and I am totally sympathetic to the work that the forensics investigators did or didn't do. I know it was a difficult task. Now, having said that, from a critical point of view, there were no forensics reports generated by any of the investigators, and I sent e-mails to the Defence on several occasions asking for copies of forensic reports and was told that there were none available. With that in mind, I cannot comment on the work that was done by any forensics investigators because to the best of my knowledge there were -- there is no work that was done. The investigators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No work or no report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No work or no reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No reports. I know of no reports. I have seen a video, and I think it was probably the first time that the investigators visited the crime scene. I think it was around 2001, but, again, I'm not sure because there's no report to document that. In that video, they take exterior shots of the house on Pionirska. They go right up to the door, ready to enter into the crime scene, and for some reason they go no further. Now, why they didn't do that, I don't know, but they chose to stop the cameras, go back, and take other shots of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, let me just interrupt you. What would an absence of forensic materials mean?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: An absence of forensic materials is basically there is no physical evidence that can be linked from the crime scene to either the indictment or trial. There's no physical evidence of anything that is accepted in a court of law. Because once you as a law enforcement agency have approached that crime scene, if you leave the scene before the scene is processed, it's generally considered from that point forward that the scene has been abandoned, and any evidence that is obtained subsequent to the time that the scene has been released is of no value.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Let's take a hypothetical investigation that you would be leading. What steps would you take from the beginning to the end in investigating the scene of the crime?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Okay. Hypothetically, what you would do is upon arrival at the scene, you would want to photographically document the exterior of the crime scene. You would want to prepare a sketch of the crime scene for the investigator's notes as to where he located specific pieces of evidence; and before the search of the scene for evidence commenced, you would want to take a tape measure and physically measure the size of the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why would you want to do that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: So when the evidence was located, you can then go back again with your tape measure and locate where in that crime scene that particular piece of evidence was located. So if necessary, a forensics investigator could come been the Tribunal and accurately tell the members of the Tribunal at what specific point in the room a particular piece of evidence was found. It may or may not be important to the case. That's not up to the investigator to determine. That is up to the learned body, the Tribunal to give whatever weight to the evidence they see fit.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Proceed with the next step that you'd take.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: So once the area has been measured, then we want to do a quick visual inventory in the crime scene to see if there's any items of evidence that are immediately available or immediately noticed by the investigator. So, for example - again, a hypothetical - let's just take a normal homicide scene, not necessarily one that's involved here but just a normal homicide. If you go into the room or you open the door to the room, you've already, you know, made your drawings and everything, and you see a gun sitting in the middle of the floor, it's obvious that that gun is probably going be a piece of evidence; either could be self-defence, could be the murder weapon, we don't know. We would want to locate that weapon in the diagram, and we would do that by measuring two points, two known points within the crime scene, and we would then triangulate the location of that weapon. So if -- for example, if I went along the south wall of a room, and I said from the door jamb 18 inches to the west along the south wall and to a point 3 feet to the north, then we would know one of the axis for the location of that weapon. Then I would go to the east wall, do the same thing. From the corner to I point parallel with the weapon, it's this distance; and from that point to the weapon, is so far. By doing that, now I have actually put the weapon in a cross, as you will, and I can go back to that room and I can put that weapon in the exact location that it was at the time that we conducted the search. Now, in this particular scene, it is a cold crime scene. I mean, it's beyond cold. These weapons --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Can I just stop you and ask you what you mean by cold crime scene?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: A cold crime scene implies that there's been an extended period of time between the actual events that took place and the time that the forensics search was done. And as time has gone on, there's a potential for cross-contamination of evidence, that being cross-contamination is a term of art, for items being brought into the crime scene from the outside that really have no relevancy to the crime scene itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As in cold case on TV.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. That's exactly what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What types of materials would cross-contaminate a scene as you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Could be anything. It really depends on the type of scene. In our hypothetical homicide, it could be trace evidence such as hair. It could be trace evidence like fibres. I mean, there's really -- in our hypothetical, we're talking about a fairly sterile crime scene. If it's indoors, you know, there's not going to be a lot of cross-contamination initially. This particular scene is kind of a combination of indoor-outdoor. It's indoor in the fact that the crime scene is protected from most of the elements, but at the same time there's a lot of problems inside the environment of the crime scene inside, and that causes particular problems for a forensic investigator in the way that they would approach that crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And right now you're speaking about Pionirska specifically.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. But let's talk about time. Let's talk about time and when the availability of the scene came about. Given that there was a war in the region, obviously there was not time to get at this scene or any of the Pionirska, Bikavac, or Varda right away. When people were available to go in, how much time would they have needed to be there in hours, days, weeks, months, years?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS
utterances.text: Let me first address an issue that deals really with Pionirska. This combination that we'd talked about of indoor-outdoor scene, it is covered, but at the same time there are a lot of environmental concerns in that area. And I am sensitive to the fact that this was a war zone at the time. But having said that, I've also seen photographs of troops that accompanied the investigators there in the year 2001. So it wasn't that -- it wasn't that it couldn't have been processed. It would have just required a security detail to help secure the scene, and then forensics could have been done. Now, having said that, to properly -- to properly process that scene would probably take in the area of two days, and the reason I say that is not because of the walls or the ceiling. Those could all be done within a matter of hours. The problem is the floor. It is not a hard floor. It is a dirt sub-floor. And what we would have to do to really do that job correctly would be to grid off the floor in, say, 1-metre squares and then take the soil down anywhere from 8 inches to 12 inches, remove that flooring, that sub-floor, and run that through a screen box to see if there was any bone fragments, teeth, jewellery, any documents, anything like that that would help to identify, number 1, that a crime did occur at the scene; and, number 2, if it did occur, is there a possibility that we could obtain evidence that would be useful in the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thanks, Ms. O'Leary. We're going to break now. Mr. Jenkins, I'd like you to leave, and you'll return tomorrow. Is it in the morning? We are on all day at 8.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry, could the Chamber kindly advise Mr. Jenkins that he's not to speak with anybody?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, you're familiar with court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As a witness, you're not to discuss your evidence with anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have a short matter to raise in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So tomorrow we start at 8.50.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tomorrow we start at 8.50, and after this witness's evidence we move to the next witness. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had anticipated that Mr. Rasic would attend. However, problems with arranging his travel arose, and VWS had to cancel his flight, and there was insufficient time to arrange train in advance for tomorrow, so they cancelled the flight. So we would conclude tomorrow whenever Mr. Jenkins finalises his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is exactly what I was hoping would not happen, that we are not able to utilize the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I worked so hard to get my colleagues to give me their trial time, and now we're not making use of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I can only -- I could pass you on the VWS -- you know, this is the problem, sometimes we're at the mercy of those things, as well, Your Honour. But we felt real confident. We had the flights arranged, and then it didn't pan out. So if we have to not call him and that's what it ends up being, that's what it'll have to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For Monday, you would have the subpoenaed witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Question, Your Honour, I take it? I hope. I don't have any control over the methodology of making that happen. Here was a concern that we had, Your Honours, VWS asked us for the WIF, and what a WIF is, is the witness information sheet that we normally fill out with just the people we know and can get them their passports. The complicating factor, Your Honour, is these people received a subpoena, which means of course we don't have that familiarity with the witness for purposes -- or friendly relationship with the witness, and so we're not sure how to facilitate the travel if we have to do WIFs for people that needed a subpoena to attend this court, and we would assume that there would be something in the process that would account for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just with respect to Mr. Rasic, I'm always trying to be mindful of the record. It just occurs to me to be helpful to preserve what is the reason why -- what happened with the plane? Was it the plane broken down, and Mr. Rasic was not able to abort it? Or was the decision taken that it was going to be too much trouble and the decision was taken not to call him? I think it may be important at a future time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The information I have, Your Honour, is that Mr. Rasic had -- and he demonstrated this, I guess, in previous attempts to book him to secure a support person, and he has a fear of flying, and I experienced this with him because I flew with him to Austria in the summertime. And so when that was disapproved, there was no time to reschedule him, and he actually said, I'll get in a car and we can video-link from Belgrade and actually volunteered to drive from Austria to Belgrade. However, we had not made the requisite application to the Court for video-link, so that, despite his intentions, really wasn't able to be facilitated between yesterday and today, so that's the situation we're in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I just clarify. This is the same Vladimir Rasic who played basketball for a university in Florida, went to university in the United States?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: For a junior college, I believe, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, one result of our not sitting tomorrow afternoon, since I presume we'll conclude with this witness in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's a possibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, in that case I better not say what the result might be. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 8.50.
